title: Gest model
text: The gossil::gest_model module holds the Gest domain model. It has one record type for each Gest entity, and the primitive values that those records use. The storage adapters and the issue commands will share these types. Storage and commands for these records remain planned. Gest is a task and artifact tracker. Gossil ports it onto Fossil mechanisms. The module is a copy of the src/store/model folder of Gest at commit eaf821b, under the MIT licence of Gest. The licence text is in src/gest_model/gest-LICENSE.txt. In the rest of this page, the pin means that commit.

title: Gest model
text: Each submodule keeps the upstream name of its record, Model, and of its inputs New, Patch and Filter where upstream has them: Records. The submodules are artifact, author, entity_tag, iteration, note, project, relationship, tag and task. Each record has private fields and a getter for each field, with the name and return type of upstream. Primitives. The primitives submodule holds Id, TaskStatus, IterationStatus, AuthorType, EntityType, RelationshipType and Priority. Each keeps its upstream variants, Display text, parser, serde spelling and methods, such as is_terminal and inverse. An Id is 16 random bytes, written as 32 letters from k to z. Id::new takes the bytes from the random source of the operating system. The constructors Author::new, Tag::new, Project::new and entity_tag::Model::new read the system clock, as upstream does.

title: Gest model
section: Build a model from a validated record
text: Gest decodes each record from a row of its own SQL tables. Gossil has no such tables. Instead, a converter in a gossil::gest_*_values module validates the decoded fields of a record. Then From moves the validated record into its model. The conversion cannot fail, because the converter has checked each field. use gossil::gest_model::{primitives::TaskStatus, task}; use gossil::gest_task_values::{TaskValueInputs, task_from_values}; use serde_json::json; let record = task_from_values(TaskValueInputs { gest_id: json!("zyxwvutsrqponmlkzyxwvutsrqponmlk"), project_id: json!("kkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkk"), title: json!("Review"), priority: json!(255), status: json!("IN_PROGRESS"), description: json!(""), assigned_to: json!(null), metadata: json!({}), resolved_at: json!(null), created_at: json!("2026-11-18T07:00:00-05:00"), updated_at: json!("2026-11-18T12:00:00Z"), }) .unwrap(); let model = task::Model::from(record); assert_eq!(model.status(), TaskStatus::InProgress); assert_eq!(serde_json::to_value(&model).unwrap()["status"], "inprogress"); The task, artifact, iteration, author, tag, note, relationship and entity tag records each have this conversion. The project record has none, because its canonical fields leave out the root. The root is a local checkout binding, and Gossil never publishes it. A caller that holds the root builds the project with Project::from_synced_parts.

title: Gest model
section: The converters and the model parse the same text
text: The converters and the model accept the same text, because the converters use the parsers of the primitives. An identifier passes a converter only when Id parses it. A task status, an iteration status, an author type, an entity type and a relationship type pass only when the parser of their primitive accepts them. The converters keep their own error messages, which name the field and do not repeat the input. The validated converter records hold the primitives, and the port did not change the converter output. The Display text and the serde spelling differ for one value. Display writes the in-progress task status as in-progress, which is the stored spelling. Serde writes it as inprogress, which is the spelling of the Gest API. The parser accepts both, and also in_progress, in any case.

title: Gest model
text: The port keeps the upstream types, names and behavior, with these exceptions: No row decoding. The TryFrom  implementations are not here. The From conversions above take their place. No local bookkeeping models. The project_workspace and transaction models are not here. They hold local workspace registrations and the local undo history, which the storage tasks own. Fallible identifier decoding. Upstream decodes an Id from serde through From , which panics on invalid text. Here, invalid text is a decoding error. From  and From  still panic on invalid text, as upstream does, so use str::parse for text from outside. Getters by hand. Upstream derives the getters with the getset crate. Here they are written out, with the same names and return types. No new clock feature. chrono has no clock feature in Gossil. The constructors read std::time::SystemTime, as chrono::Utc::now does. Random bytes from getrandom. Upstream uses rand.

title: Gest model
text: The tests hold the 77 inherited Gest tests of the model files at the pin. Most of them are in tests/gest_model.rs. Four identifier tests use private items, so they stay next to the code in src/gest_model/primitives/id.rs. The bodies of the tests are the upstream bodies. Only the imports change, and the project test reads the clock without chrono::Utc::now. One inherited test checks the excluded project_workspace model, and it is not ported. The source map tests/fixtures/gest_model/source-map.json names the port of each inherited test, with the test ID, assertion IDs and fixture hash from the Gest test inventory. It also cites each ported Gest file with its hash at the pin. A test compares those hashes with the shared table in tests/support/gest_source_map.rs. It fails when a copy of the map has a stale or malformed entry. Another test checks that each model test that a converter map lists as a later obligation is a test that the model map ports. Other new tests check the serde spellings and the constructors that read the clock. They also check that a bad identifier gives an error and not a panic, and that each validated record converts into its model. The module defines no repository traits, storage, commands or web routes. The model inputs New, Patch and Filter are plain data, and no code reads them yet.

title: Gest model

title: Gest note values

The converter does not read a clock, generate an identifier, look up references or execute SQL. use gossil::gest_note_values::{NoteValueInputs, note_from_values, note_to_values}; use serde_json::json; let fields = NoteValueInputs { gest_id: json!("klmnopqrstuvwxyzklmnopqrstuvwxyz"), entity_id: json!("zyxwvutsrqponmlkzyxwvutsrqponmlk"), entity_type: json!("Task"), author_id: json!(null), body: json!("Checked the *build*.\n"), created_at: json!("2026-11-18T07:00:00-05:00"), updated_at: json!("2026-11-18T12:00:00Z"), }; let record = note_from_values(fields).unwrap(); let output = note_to_values(&record); assert_eq!(output.entity_type, json!("task")); assert_eq!(output.author_id, json!(null)); assert_eq!(output.created_at, json!("2026-11-18T12:00:00+00:00")); assert_eq!(note_from_values(output).unwrap(), record);

title: Gest note values
text: The note ID and the entity ID must each contain exactly 32 lowercase letters from k through z. The author ID is JSON null for an unknown author, or a full ID of the same form. The converter keeps null as null. An empty string is not an unknown author, so it fails. The entity type accepts artifact, iteration and task. Gest ignores case when it parses an entity type. So the converter accepts Task and returns the lowercase spelling. A project, a tag and an author are not entity types here. Surrounding whitespace fails. It converts each timestamp to UTC and checks that the output can be parsed again. It does not check the order of the two timestamps. NoteValueError displays the field and a static reason, and does not repeat the input. Its parse_cause() accessor returns the chrono error from the parse of the input or from the parse of the canonical UTC output. Other failures have no parser cause. Callers own raw decoding, required-field presence, unknown-field classification, duplicate keys in the original input and byte budgets. Callers also check that the entity and the author exist in the selected project, and they check the complete history of changes to the record. The converter does not implement lifecycle, replay, migration, storage or the complete Gest API.

The issue ticket writer stores a project privately. The command gos i init builds a new project with this module and stores it that way. The other CLI commands remain planned. title: Gest project values
text: Before constructing serde_json::Value inputs, callers check raw JSON for required fields, unknown fields and duplicate keys. Duplicate keys must be checked before decoding collapses them. Then assemble every field for conversion. Nullable archive state requires an explicit null. The converter does not read a clock, generate an identifier, look up references or execute SQL. use gossil::gest_project_values::{ProjectValueInputs, project_from_values, project_to_values}; use serde_json::json; let fields = ProjectValueInputs { gest_id: json!("kkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkk"), archived_at: json!(null), created_at: json!("2026-11-18T07:00:00-05:00"), updated_at: json!("2025-01-01T00:00:00Z"), }; let project = project_from_values(fields).unwrap(); let values = project_to_values(&project); assert_eq!(values.created_at, json!("2026-11-18T12:00:00+00:00")); assert_eq!(project_from_values(values).unwrap(), project); The example sets modification before creation to show that conversion imposes no time ordering.

title: Gest project values
text: The identifier must contain exactly 32 lowercase letters from k through z. Archive state accepts null or an RFC3339 timestamp. Creation and modification timestamps require strings. ProjectValueError displays the field and a static reason without echoing input. Its parse_cause() accessor retains the actual chrono error from input parsing or canonical UTC output parsing. Relationship persistence and CLI commands remain planned. Gest is a task and artifact tracker. A Gest relationship is one directed link from a source entity to a target entity, for example a task that blocks another task. Each entity is a task, an artifact or an iteration. Here, canonical means the eight relationship fields in the reviewed field map. In a source checkout, the map is tests/fixtures/gest_relationship_values/source-map.json. title: Gest relationship values
text: Before you build the serde_json::Value inputs, check the raw JSON for required fields, unknown fields and duplicate keys. Check duplicate keys before decoding, because decoding merges them. Then assemble every field for conversion. The converter does not read a clock, generate an identifier, look up references or execute SQL. use gossil::gest_relationship_values::{ RelationshipValueInputs, relationship_from_values, relationship_to_values, }; use serde_json::json; let fields = RelationshipValueInputs { gest_id: json!("klmnopqrstuvwxyzklmnopqrstuvwxyz"), rel_type: json!("Child-Of"), source_id: json!("kkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkk"), source_type: json!("task"), target_id: json!("zzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzz"), target_type: json!("TASK"), created_at: json!("2026-11-18T07:00:00-05:00"), updated_at: json!("2026-11-18T12:00:00Z"), }; let record = relationship_from_values(fields).unwrap(); let output = relationship_to_values(&record); assert_eq!(output.rel_type, json!("child-of")); assert_eq!(output.target_type, json!("task")); assert_eq!(output.created_at, json!("2026-11-18T12:00:00+00:00")); assert_eq!(relationship_from_values(output).unwrap(), record);

title: Gest relationship values
text: The relationship ID, the source ID and the target ID must each contain exactly 32 lowercase letters from k through z. The source type and the target type accept artifact, iteration and task. The relationship type accepts the five Gest spellings blocked-by, blocks, child-of, parent-of and relates-to. Gest ignores case when it parses a relationship type or an entity type. So the converter accepts Child-Of, and the output is the lowercase spelling. Underscore spellings such as child_of and surrounding whitespace fail. The record keeps the direction as given. Gest pairs each type with an inverse type. blocks and blocked-by are inverses, child-of and parent-of are inverses, and relates-to is its own inverse. The converter does not apply the inverse and does not create the inverse row. A row from A to B and a row from B to A are two different records. Both timestamps must be strings. The shared timestamp validation uses chrono 0.4.44. It converts each timestamp to UTC and checks that the output can be parsed again. It does not check the order of the two timestamps. Upstream, the directed tuple of type, source type, source ID, target type and target ID is unique among all relationships. A single record cannot show a duplicate, so the converter does not check uniqueness. The Gossil contract GEST-CONSTRAINT-01 requires that check across all live relationship records. Gossil does not implement this check yet. RelationshipValueError displays the field and a static reason, and does not repeat the input. Its parse_cause() accessor returns the chrono error from the parse of the input or from the parse of the canonical UTC output. Other failures have no parser cause. Callers own raw decoding, required-field presence, unknown-field classification, duplicate keys in the original input, byte budgets and the uniqueness of the directed tuple. Callers also check that both endpoints exist in the selected project, and they check the complete history of changes to the record. The converter does not implement lifecycle, replay, migration, storage or the complete Gest API.

title: Gest relationship values
text: The ten converter controls in tests/gest_relationship_values.rs check complete output, independent ownership, types, identifiers, type spellings, direction and timestamp boundaries with typed causes. They also include the hash of the test accounting addendum. The control then makes copies of the map, each with one stale or malformed entry, and checks that the comparison refuses each copy. The Gest files are not in this repository, so the control compares the hashes that the map records with these values. It does not hash the files themselves. These tests cover the converter itself. They do not reproduce the upstream relationship API or repository tests. The source map lists 15 upstream enum tests as later API obligations. Five test the EntityType enum, and ten test the RelationshipType enum, including its five inverse tests. The converter uses the Display and FromStr methods of both enums, through their ports in the Gest model. It does not use inverse. The tests of the model port run the 15 tests.

Tag persistence and CLI commands remain planned. Gest is a task and artifact tracker. A Gest tag is a label that Gest stores once and attaches to tasks, artifacts and iterations. It is not a Fossil control tag. Here, canonical means the four tag fields in the reviewed field map. In a source checkout, the map is tests/fixtures/gest_tag_values/source-map.json. TagValueInputs requires an explicit serde_json::Value for gest_id, label, created_at and updated_at. tag_from_values returns a TagValues record with private fields. tag_to_values returns all four fields as independent owned values. The upstream tag model defines the source record. See library setup for Cargo dependencies.

title: Gest tag values
text: Before you build the serde_json::Value inputs, check the raw JSON for required fields, unknown fields and duplicate keys. Check duplicate keys before decoding, because decoding merges them. Then assemble every field for conversion. The converter does not read a clock, generate an identifier, look up references or execute SQL. use gossil::gest_tag_values::{TagValueInputs, tag_from_values, tag_to_values}; use serde_json::json; let fields = TagValueInputs { gest_id: json!("klmnopqrstuvwxyzklmnopqrstuvwxyz"), label: json!("Urgent"), created_at: json!("2026-11-18T07:00:00-05:00"), updated_at: json!("2026-11-18T12:00:00Z"), }; let record = tag_from_values(fields).unwrap(); let output = tag_to_values(&record); assert_eq!(output.label, json!("Urgent")); assert_eq!(output.created_at, json!("2026-11-18T12:00:00+00:00")); assert_eq!(tag_from_values(output).unwrap(), record);

title: Gest tag values
text: The identifier must contain exactly 32 lowercase letters from k through z. The label accepts any string, including an empty string, Unicode and null characters. The converter keeps the label exactly as given, so Urgent and urgent stay two different labels. Both timestamps must be strings. The shared timestamp validation uses chrono 0.4.44. It converts each timestamp to UTC and checks that the output can be parsed again. It does not check the order of the two timestamps. Upstream, each label is unique among all tags. A single record cannot show a duplicate, so the converter does not check uniqueness. The Gossil contract GEST-CONSTRAINT-01 requires that check across all live tag records. Under that contract, two tags with equal labels and distinct IDs are a conflict. The check keeps both records, marks them as conflicts and hides the conflicted rows. Gossil does not implement the check or the hiding of those rows yet. The converter handles a single record and has no conflict state. TagValueError displays the field and a static reason, and does not repeat the input. Its parse_cause() accessor returns the chrono error from the parse of the input or from the parse of the canonical UTC output. Other failures have no parser cause. Callers own raw decoding, required-field presence, unknown-field classification, duplicate keys in the original input, byte budgets and label uniqueness. Callers also check the complete history of changes to the record. The converter does not attach tags to entities. It does not implement lifecycle, replay, migration, storage or the complete Gest API.

title: Gest tag values
text: The nine converter controls in tests/gest_tag_values.rs check complete output, independent ownership, types, identifiers, exact labels and timestamp boundaries with typed causes. One of them checks that the source map names each field, and that each control that it names exists in the file. The same control compares the map with the expected values in tests/support/gest_source_map.rs. These values are the Gest commit, the hash of each cited Gest file and the exact list of fields. They also include the hash of the test accounting addendum. The control then makes copies of the map, each with one stale or malformed entry, and checks that the comparison refuses each copy. The Gest files are not in this repository, so the control compares the hashes that the map records with these values. It does not hash the files themselves. These tests cover the converter itself. They do not reproduce the upstream tag API or repository tests. The upstream constructor test calls Model::new, which generates an ID and reads the clock. The source map lists it as a later API obligation. The Gest model ports Model::new and runs that test. The converter does not call it.

title: Gest tag values
text: Use the converter after checking the complete raw input. Next, check label uniqueness across the live tag records before you store a converted tag.

title: Gest task values
text: The gossil::gest_task_values module converts eleven already decoded task fields into an owned, validated record. Callers can use the record for complete task snapshots before storage integration. Pass validated snapshots to the task ticket emitter for bounded creation artifact bytes. The module does not implement the full Gest API or migrate stored repositories. Gest is a task and artifact tracker. This converter uses its task record model. Here, canonical values use the status and UTC timestamp forms defined below. TaskValueInputs requires an explicit serde_json::Value for each field. task_from_values validates these values and returns TaskValues, whose fields are private. task_to_values returns the complete set of owned values. The functions do not read a clock, generate identifiers or execute SQL.

title: Gest task values
text: Check raw input field presence, duplicates and byte limits before assembling decoded values. No field has a default. The public input and output use the same TaskValueInputs type. use gossil::gest_task_values::{TaskValueInputs, task_from_values, task_to_values}; use serde_json::json; let fields = TaskValueInputs { gest_id: json!("zyxwvutsrqponmlkzyxwvutsrqponmlk"), project_id: json!("kkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkk"), title: json!("Review task values"), priority: json!(255), status: json!("IN_PROGRESS"), description: json!(""), assigned_to: json!(null), metadata: json!([null, {"reviewed": false}]), resolved_at: json!(null), created_at: json!("2026-11-18T07:00:00-05:00"), updated_at: json!("2026-11-18T12:00:00Z"), }; let task = task_from_values(fields).unwrap(); let values = task_to_values(&task); assert_eq!(values.status, json!("in-progress")); assert_eq!(values.created_at, json!("2026-11-18T12:00:00+00:00")); assert_eq!(task_from_values(values).unwrap(), task); The example uses array metadata and priority 255 to show the model’s full value types. Production callers must handle TaskValueError from validation. Its display text names the first rejected field and the reason, without echoing the supplied value. TaskValueError::parse_cause() returns the original chrono::ParseError when parsing the input or its canonical UTC output fails. Callers can inspect its kind() to distinguish failures such as TooShort and OutOfRange. Other validation failures return no parse cause. Error equality includes the retained cause, so errors with equal display text can compare unequal. Chrono’s alloc-only build does not implement std::error::Error for this parser error, so callers use the accessor rather than Error::source(). The validated record stays unchanged if a caller changes the owned fields returned by task_to_values.

title: Gest task values
text: The input requires all eleven fields, even when a value is null. Field Admitted value gest_id Full task ID string, called id in Gest’s task Model. project_id Full project ID string. title Any string. priority Null or a JSON integer from 0 through 255. status A status string accepted by Gest’s task status FromStr implementation. description Any string. assigned_to Null or a full author ID string. metadata Any serde_json::Value, including null. resolved_at A timestamp string for terminal status, otherwise null. created_at A timestamp string. updated_at A timestamp string. The task and project identifiers require exactly 32 lowercase letters from k through z. An assignee is null or a full identifier. Title and description preserve their strings, including empty strings, Unicode, whitespace and null characters. The task field gest_id corresponds to upstream Model.id. Priority is null or an integer from 0 through 255. Checked conversion rejects negative integers, larger integers, floating point values and other JSON types. The upstream task model uses Option . Its separate named priority enum covers only 0 through 4 and is outside this module. Status parsing uses the parser of TaskStatus in the Gest model, which is a port of upstream FromStr. The statuses are open, in-progress, done and cancelled. Parsing accepts case differences and the in-progress, in_progress and inprogress aliases. Output uses in-progress. The adopted Gossil contract requires a resolution timestamp for done and cancelled, and null for open and in-progress. The converter checks that pairing without generating a timestamp. Metadata retains every JSON value variant, including null. Explicit metadata null is model data, independent of the nulls in optional model fields. The converter preserves JSON value semantics without promising original JSON spelling, object member order or duplicate-key detection. Business timestamps use Gest’s pinned chrono 0.4.44 RFC3339 parser and normalize to Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), subject to Gossil’s canonical output contract. RFC3339 is the timestamp string format used at this boundary. Output uses chrono’s RFC3339 form with the +00:00 offset and at most nine fractional digits. The parser accepts offsets, lowercase separators, a space separator, year zero and leap seconds. It truncates fractional input beyond nanoseconds, as upstream does. Business timestamp rules are separate from the stricter artifact D-card time grammar. The converter adds no ordering rule between timestamps. A parsed instant must have a UTC representation that the RFC3339 parser can read back. Offset normalization across the year zero or 9999 boundary can produce a signed extended year. The converter rejects those results under the adopted output contract. Upstream source parsing accepts their inputs. Year zero and nearby offsets remain valid when their UTC result is representable. The module does not claim parity with the full upstream timestamp input domain. Invalid field types, incomplete identifiers, invalid priorities or statuses, unparseable timestamps and inconsistent status/resolution pairs return TaskValueError. Normalized UTC output outside the adopted RFC3339 domain also returns that error. Metadata has no further type restriction.

title: Gest task values
text: Cargo.toml pins chrono to 0.4.44 with default features disabled. Its enabled features are alloc and serde. The Gest model needs serde to read and write its timestamps. The clock feature stays off. The lockfile includes chrono 0.4.44, num-traits 0.2.19 and autocfg 1.5.1. These additions support timestamp conversion in Rust and do not add a native Fossil process or a SQL date conversion to this module.

title: Gest task values
text: The caller must validate and decode raw fields before constructing the input. For ticket artifacts, it must classify each J card, which assigns a named field. It must check complete field presence, reject duplicate field spellings where required and enforce byte limits for the operation. The explicit input struct is not an object decoder and cannot identify fields that the caller discarded. The enclosing implementation must validate history, resolve references to other records and decide which unsupported fields or records to reject. This module supplies complete task values for before and after snapshots. The separate task ticket emitter supplies creation bytes. Applying history, recording operation recipes and the source of changes, undoing operations and writing storage remain separate work. The converter does not enable migration of stored repositories.

title: Gest task values
text: The converter follows Gest source commit eaf821b19c3cf75b99d22e1cc70e0eff4a3562a8 with the Gossil validation rules specified above. Source mappings, test counts and historical run qualifications are preserved in the task value evidence archive. Those runs qualify their recorded trees and do not establish full Gest or Fossil compatibility. The task ticket emitter takes its list of canonical fields from this module. The list borrows the title, description and metadata, and it holds short owned strings for the identifiers, the status and the timestamps. The issue ticket writer calls task_from_values on each task creation that it stores or reads. Commands do not call this module. This page follows the nossaifd writing guide, including principles credited to Rosalind Reid, Shreya Shankar and Oskar Austegard.

title: Gest task values
text: Use the explicit decoded-field converter for complete task snapshots. Next, handle TaskValueError and use task_to_values to inspect the normalized values or pass the validated record to the task ticket emitter.

title: Emit artifact and project creation tickets
text: The gest_ticket module turns a validated Gest artifact or project record into complete, uncompressed bytes in Fossil’s ticket artifact format. Gest is the issue tracker that Gossil ports. Each Gest record becomes an ordinary Fossil ticket, so stock Fossil can store, rebuild and show it. A Gest artifact is a document record, for example a spec or a plan. It is not a Fossil blob. A Gest project groups the tasks, artifacts and iterations of one piece of work. Planned work also uses the artifact ticket. A logical change is a stable name for future work on an issue. The planned-changes contract CHANGE-01 uses an artifact ticket to carry each logical change. Use the library to inspect or test these creation artifacts in memory. The issue ticket writer stores a project creation privately in a native repository. The attachment that declares a logical change and the storage of artifact tickets remain separate work. So do the issue commands other than gos i init, gos i task create, gos i task list and gos i task show.

title: Emit artifact and project creation tickets
text: Validate the decoded fields first, with artifact_from_values or project_from_values. The artifact values guide and the project values guide show that step. Then emit the artifact with an explicit byte limit: use gossil::gest_artifact_values::{ArtifactValueInputs, artifact_from_values}; use gossil::gest_ticket::artifact_creation_bytes; use gossil::native_date::NativeDate; use serde_json::json; let artifact = artifact_from_values(ArtifactValueInputs { gest_id: json!("zyxwvutsrqponmlkzyxwvutsrqponmlk"), project_id: json!("kkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkk"), title: json!("Plan"), body: json!("Complete body"), metadata: json!({}), archived_at: json!(null), created_at: json!("2026-11-18T12:00:00Z"), updated_at: json!("2026-11-18T12:00:00Z"), }) .unwrap(); let date = NativeDate::parse(b"2026-11-18T12:00:00Z").unwrap(); let ticket_id = b"0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567"; let bytes = artifact_creation_bytes(&artifact, ticket_id, b"native actor", date, 65_536).unwrap(); assert!(bytes.len() <= 65_536); project_creation_bytes takes a ProjectValues record and the same four other arguments. In an application, handle TicketError and do not unwrap the result.

title: Emit artifact and project creation tickets
text: A ticket artifact is a sequence of newline-terminated records called cards. Each emitted artifact has a D card, the sorted J cards, a K card, a U card and a final Z card: D holds the creation date in the native date grammar. J assigns one named field to its encoded value. K holds the ticket identity, exactly forty lowercase ASCII hexadecimal bytes. U holds the actor bytes, escaped with the token codec. Z holds the lowercase MD5 checksum of all the bytes before it. The caller supplies K independently of the record’s gest_id. A Gest ID has 32 lowercase letters from k through z and stays a J field. The emitter neither generates identities nor derives one identity from the other.

title: Emit artifact and project creation tickets
text: The J value of each model field is the compact serde_json encoding of the converter output, followed by native token escaping. The converter output is the value of artifact_to_values or project_to_values. Strings keep their JSON quotes, metadata keeps its JSON value, and null values stay present. Timestamps use the UTC form +00:00. Kind Model fields J cards artifact archived_at, body, created_at, gest_id, metadata, project_id, title, updated_at 11 project archived_at, created_at, gest_id, updated_at 7 Each artifact also has the three fixed fields of the task ticket. gossil_deleted is JSON false. gossil_kind is the raw kind name, artifact or project, and gossil_schema is raw 1. The J cards are sorted by name. The field names are the Gest table columns, with id renamed to gest_id. The artifact body keeps its exact text. A non-null archived_at does not mark a record as deleted. The project’s local checkout root is not a canonical field, so a project ticket does not include the path of the local checkout.

title: Emit artifact and project creation tickets
text: The task, artifact and project emitters call one crate-private function. Each kind gives only its sorted list of fields and its kind name. So the three kinds share the card syntax, the size plan, the limit checks and the checksum. The task ticket guide describes the same rules for tasks. It also describes max_output. The shared emitter does not change the task bytes, and two task fixtures hold the expected bytes. The first fixture was spelled by hand before the shared emitter existed, and the second fills every task field. max_output bounds the complete encoded artifact. An exact-size limit succeeds, and a smaller limit returns TicketError::Size. The emitter counts the encoded size of the borrowed title, body and metadata before it copies them. A test checks that a 256 KiB body over the limit causes no allocation of 4096 bytes or more. This module defines TicketError, and task_ticket re-exports it. Its Size message is ticket output limit, because all three kinds return the error.

title: Emit artifact and project creation tickets
text: tests/gest_ticket.rs covers both kinds: Golden bytes. Each kind matches a fixture that tests/fixtures/gest-ticket/generate.py spells by hand. The same script also writes both task fixtures of tests/task_ticket.rs. Round trips. Each record survives the structural parser, then the converter again, for row GEST-T01 of the Gest contract. Field mapping. The J names equal the canonical field names in the committed converter source maps. Each J value equals the JSON bytes of the converter output. Limits. An oversized title, body or metadata value fails before a large allocation. just gest-ticket-interop runs the stock Fossil check. It loads one artifact, one project and one task ticket into a scratch repository of the pinned Fossil 2.29 at 7e8ecf0ce4. The repository has one ticket column for each Gest field. After a full rebuild, the test checks these results: test-integrity --parse finds no error. ticket show returns each J value byte for byte. ticket history lists each field change. artifact returns the emitted bytes. If the Fossil reference binary is absent, the recipe prints not-run and exits with status 5. A not-run result is not a pass. The test never calls fossil ticket add, because that command can crash in Fossil 2.29 at tkt.c:1862.

title: Emit artifact and project creation tickets
text: Check raw field presence, duplicate keys and input byte limits before you construct a record. Choose the ticket identity, actor, D instant and output limit independently of the model fields. The emitter reads no clock, generates no identity and writes no database. It does not replay history, check references or decide who may write a record. A future repository operation must enforce these rules, including any rule that artifact dates increase. This page follows the nossaifd writing guide, including principles credited to Rosalind Reid, Shreya Shankar and Oskar Austegard.

title: Emit artifact and project creation tickets
text: Validate a record with its converter, then call artifact_creation_bytes or project_creation_bytes with an explicit output limit. Run just gest-ticket-interop after a change to the emitter, and report not-run apart from a pass. Store a project with the issue ticket writer. The storage of artifact tickets and the declaration of a logical change remain planned.

title: Get started
text: Use Gossil to create a delta between two files and restore the target exactly. A delta encodes target bytes as new bytes and copies from an origin file. This exercise needs no repository and does not change Git history. Gossil is intended to keep agent files, issues and their history alongside Git. Its command line initializes and opens repositories, tracks explicit files, selects their scopes, records private history and has three delta diagnostics. The Rust library also supports artifact parsing, local storage and task, project and author conversion. Try the delta commands below. Read working with repositories for the intended file and issue workflows.

title: Get started
text: Install Git, Rust with Cargo, Just, uv and the jlog command recorder. These tools must be available on PATH. Rust builds also need the native compiler and platform development tools used by Cargo dependencies. Linux setup also requires Make, zlib development headers and CA certificates to build the pinned Tcl and Fossil references. On other hosts, supply the reference prerequisites before setup. The commands below use a POSIX shell, such as the default shell on macOS or Linux. git clone https://github.com/rahuldave/gossil.git cd gossil just setup just setup supplies the Linux references or checks the existing tools on other hosts, then fetches the Cargo dependencies. just gossil then builds and runs the source executable through jlog and Cargo. You do not need a globally installed gossil executable. The first build can take longer than later calls. The example builds from source. Keep the checkout open in this shell for the following commands. The contributor setup is for people who also need the optional workflow packages and verification guidance.

title: Get started
text: Make a fresh scratch folder so that the example cannot overwrite earlier work. Keep the quotation marks around paths so that paths with spaces work too. example_dir=$(mktemp -d /tmp/gossil-example.XXXXXX) printf 'before\n' > "$example_dir/origin" printf 'after\n' > "$example_dir/target" just gossil vcs test-delta-create "$example_dir/origin" "$example_dir/target" "$example_dir/change.delta" The arguments are the original file, the desired file, and the delta to write. Success writes change.delta and prints no command output. Cargo can print build messages on stderr. A delta need not be smaller than its target, especially for small files like these.

title: Get started
text: Apply the delta to the same origin, writing a separate restored file: just gossil vcs test-delta-apply "$example_dir/origin" "$example_dir/change.delta" "$example_dir/restored" cmp "$example_dir/target" "$example_dir/restored" cat "$example_dir/restored" cmp prints nothing and exits with status 0 when the files match. cat prints after. The original and target files remain available. To check that Gossil can create and apply deltas in both directions, run: just gossil vcs test-delta "$example_dir/origin" "$example_dir/target" Success prints ok. This command checks the round trip in memory. It does not save another delta or create a check-in. You can repeat these commands with text or binary files. A delta describes bytes, so keep its matching origin when you need to restore the target later.

title: Get started
text: v is the short name for vcs: just gossil v test-delta "$example_dir/origin" "$example_dir/target" The source also builds a gos executable with the same diagnostics. See short executable names for its source invocation. The same aliases support native checkout open. The issue group, or i, recognises the Gest command names. It runs init, which creates the Gest project of an open checkout. It also runs task create, which adds a private task to that project. task list and task show read its tasks. It refuses each other command with status 69. The other issue commands, shared recording and sync remain planned. The issue guide walks through these commands beside check-ins, and reads the result with stock Fossil.

title: Get started
section: Handle failures and choose the next step
text: A diagnostic exits with status 1 and writes an error to stderr when it fails. Check the input paths and argument order first. If applying a delta fails, check that you kept the correct origin and an intact delta. The CLI reference lists the exact messages. An unknown command exits with status 2. Run just gossil --help to list the commands, or add --help after a command to print its usage. Successful create and apply operations replace an existing output file. Use a fresh output path until you have checked the result. Validation failures preserve the output, but a write failure can leave it truncated. The repository guide explains how a file delta differs from a check-in and how Gossil is intended to work beside Git. For application code, use the library examples and generated Rust API. The application manifest must select Gossil’s bundled libSQL provider as shown in those examples. The provider implements the Fossil date arithmetic required by artifact parsing and repository validation.

title: Get started
text: Choose a destination that does not exist: just gossil vcs init --admin-user alice example.gossil The receipt gives the project and server identifiers and the initial administrator password. Save the password privately. This command creates the empty root without a checkout or tracked files. It reads no preference file. See the initialization reference for date, hash and login options. An already installed mini-VCS preview has a separate command contract. These commands build the current source.

title: Get started
text: After the initialization above, create a directory and register it from source: mkdir example-work just gossil vcs open --repository example.gossil --checkout work --root example-work Open registers the initial empty root and writes a local lookup file, example-work/.gossil/checkout.json. Commands use that file to find and verify the checkout. It selects no files and requires no issue, project or author initialization. Configuration, permissions and existing markers can refuse the operation. Read native checkout open before retrying a failure, because database commit and locator publication have distinct outcomes.

title: Get started
text: Use add and status to enroll exact file paths. Add stores tracking metadata without changing working files or storing file content. Status lists every tracked path with its pending or recorded state and actual scope. New paths have unselected scope. The scope and commit commands select immutable scopes and record the complete private tracked tree. The development guide records the qualification boundary between source, release and installation.

title: Get started
text:
Start in the Gossil source repository root after setup. This example runs gos through Cargo and keeps its database outside the working root. It uses absolute paths, so later commands can run inside the registered checkout. Existing Gest configuration must satisfy the open contract. recording_source=$(pwd -P) recording_trial=$(mktemp -d /tmp/gossil-recording.XXXXXX) recording_gos() { cargo run --locked --manifest-path "$recording_source/Cargo.toml" --bin gos -- "$@" } mkdir "$recording_trial/work" recording_gos v init --admin-user alice --date-override '2026-11-20 00:00:00' "$recording_trial/history.gossil" recording_gos v open --repository "$recording_trial/history.gossil" --checkout work --root "$recording_trial/work" cd "$recording_trial/work" printf 'first plan
' > plan.md printf 'first review
' > review.md recording_gos v add --repository "$recording_trial/history.gossil" --checkout work --path plan.md --path review.md recording_gos v scope --repository "$recording_trial/history.gossil" --checkout work --scope private --path plan.md --path review.md recording_gos v commit --repository "$recording_trial/history.gossil" --checkout work --scope private --all-tracked --user alice --comment 'Save notes' --date-override '2026-11-21T12:00:00' printf 'revised plan
' > plan.md recording_gos v commit --repository "$recording_trial/history.gossil" --checkout work --scope private --all-tracked --user alice --comment 'Revise plan' --date-override '2026-11-22T12:00:00' recording_gos v open --repository "$recording_trial/history.gossil" --checkout work recording_gos v status --repository "$recording_trial/history.gossil" --checkout work recording_gos v commit --repository "$recording_trial/history.gossil" --checkout work --scope private --all-tracked --user alice --comment 'Check unchanged tree' --date-override '2026-11-23T12:00:00' Scope prints Selected scopes: 2. Each changed commit prints Recorded private check-in: HASH, where HASH identifies that check-in. The final commit prints No changes. Each output ends with a newline. Status lists both paths as R with private scope. It does not report live edits. The second commit captures the edit without re-adding the file. Reopen preserves the files and private history, and the shared head still names the empty root. These dates follow the deterministic root and each previous parent. Use later valid dates for subsequent commits, including no-change checks. Comments must not contain [, even when the tree is unchanged. A nonzero exit after an output failure can leave a durable commit. Retry the same binding with unchanged files and valid later metadata. A previously recorded tree yields No changes. See the failure contract. This walkthrough describes current source and does not install a default executable.

title: Get started
text: From the source walkthrough checkout above, use its recording_gos helper: recording_gos vcs info --repository "$recording_trial/history.gossil" --checkout work The command prints the supplied repository path and canonical checkout root as JSON strings, then the current checkout, shared head and private head. Before a private recording, the private head is none and checkout equals the shared head. After a private recording, checkout equals the private combined head. Edits without a commit do not change these recorded IDs. See the exact info contract for output and failure rules.

title: Get started
text: From the source walkthrough checkout, run: recording_gos vcs timeline --repository "$recording_trial/history.gossil" --checkout work recording_gos v log --checkout work --repository "$recording_trial/history.gossil" Both commands print the same three compact JSON rows for the revised private check-in, the first private check-in and the shared empty root, in that order. Each row ends with LF and contains hash, date, actor, comment and private, in that order. The no-change retry added no row. Hashes are complete, and the original metadata is preserved with standard JSON escaping. The root alone has private: false. The commands need a complete matching locator. They do not read working-file contents, select revisions or accept filters. See the ancestry command contract for bounds and failures. This walkthrough builds source and supplies no installation evidence.

title: Get started
section: Inspect a glob list from source
text: The diagnostic accepts literal pattern lists and candidates without a repository. The 2026-11-21 focused checkpoint built and exercised the source interface. Its full qualification limits are separate from this example. Return to the Gossil source root before running this command. just gossil vcs test-glob '*.rs,src/*' src/lib.rs notes.md The shell quotes keep the pattern list in one argument. The diagnostic prints SQL, parsed patterns and both match indices. It selects no tracked files. Read the CLI grammar and glob contract before using it. The default installed development preview is a separate build, and this source example does not update it.

title: Get started
text: Use disposable copies for the source private recording walkthrough. Next, inspect status, edit a tracked copy and commit again with a later explicit date.

title: Git reader
text: The gossil::git_reader module reads a Git repository beside Git, and it never writes to Git. Binding is the step that ties a Gossil change to a Git commit. GIT-01 of the Git access contract lists the reads that binding needs, and the module does each of them. It finds the Git directory of a worktree, reads HEAD and a branch tip, and reads a commit with its ordered parents. It also reads the object format and three keys of the configuration. The section The guards against writes gives the checks that keep the module from writing. The module is a library only. No command uses it yet. The bind command, the hooks and the storage of the source registry are separate work.

title: Git reader
text: GitRepository::open(worktree, limits) opens one worktree. A worktree is a folder with checked-out files and a .git entry. The folder must hold the .git entry itself. The reader searches no parent folder, and it reads no Git environment variable, such as GIT_DIR. Call Result GitRepository::open(path, Limits::STANDARD) The opened repository, after the support checks below. repo.worktree() The canonical top folder of the worktree, which holds .git. repo.git_dir() The Git directory of the worktree, which holds its HEAD. repo.common_dir() The common Git directory, which holds the objects, the shared refs and config. repo.is_linked_worktree() True when the two directories differ. repo.object_format() ObjectFormat::Sha1 or ObjectFormat::Sha256. repo.config() The three configuration keys, as RepositoryConfig. A main worktree has .git as a folder, and its Git directory is the common directory. A linked worktree, which git worktree add makes, has a .git file. The file names a folder below .git/worktrees of the main repository, and that folder names the common directory in its file commondir. The reader drops only the line ends, \n and \r, at the end of commondir. So a space stays a part of the path.

title: Git reader
text: GitRepository::open checks the repository against the table below at each call, because git refs migrate can change a repository between two runs. It returns an error for an unsupported repository before any other read, and the error names the reason. Repository Result of the open SHA-1 or SHA-256, files ref backend, loose or packed objects, alternates, linked worktrees Opened A multi-pack-index Opened; the reader reads the packs without the index Folder without a .git entry, which is not a bare repository GitReadError::NotAWorktree .git entry that does not lead to a valid Git directory, a .git file that names a file and not a folder, or a HEAD that names a ref outside refs/ GitReadError::NotARepository .git file whose path ends in whitespace, such as from git init --separate-git-dir "gd " GitReadError::NotARepository, because gix would strip the space and open another folder HEAD that Git calls broken, such as a short ID or an ID with data after it GitReadError::Ref .git, HEAD, config, commondir or alternates that is a FIFO, a device, a socket, a dangling link or a refused link GitReadError::NotAFile objects/info/alternates over its limits, an alternate that is not a folder, or an alternate that gix reads otherwise than Git, as Limits says GitReadError::Alternate, or TooLarge for the size Shallow clone, or a linked worktree of one GitReadError::Shallow, because the common directory holds the file shallow extensions.refStorage=reftable GitReadError::Reftable Bare repository of either format, also with a detached HEAD, or a worktree for which core.bare is true GitReadError::Bare, because a bare repository is not a location of the source registry Linked worktree of a bare repository, without extensions.worktreeConfig Opened, because Git does not treat the linked worktree as bare Worktree whose core.worktree names another folder GitReadError::ForeignWorktree, because Git’s worktree is that other folder Unknown object format, unknown ref backend UnsupportedObjectFormat or UnsupportedRefStorage core.repositoryformatversion other than 0 or 1 UnsupportedRepositoryVersion Version 0 with an extension that Git knows only in version 1 UnsupportedRepositoryVersion, as in Git Version 1 with an extension that Git does not know, or with extensions.compatObjectFormat UnsupportedExtension extensions.objectFormat, refStorage, partialClone or compatObjectFormat without a value GitReadError::Config, as in Git The reader checks the keys below extensions as Git’s setup.c does, in upper or lower case: Git knows noop, preciousObjects, partialClone and worktreeConfig in both versions. Git knows noop-v1, objectFormat, compatObjectFormat, refStorage, relativeWorktrees and submodulePathConfig only in version 1, and it stops with an error on them in version 0. In version 0, Git ignores an unknown key, and so does the reader. In version 1, Git stops with an error on an unknown key. A key in a subsection, such as [extensions "x"] noop, is unknown. The reader also returns UnsupportedExtension for compatObjectFormat, which it does not support. A partial clone opens. A commit that is not present gives GitReadError::ObjectMissing. core.worktree names the worktree, relative to the Git directory. The open returns an error for a value that does not lead to the opened folder. The reader takes core.bare and core.worktree from the files that Git reads, as git rev-parse shows: config.worktree of the worktree, when extensions.worktreeConfig is true, wins over the common config. The common config applies to a main worktree. It applies to a linked worktree only when extensions.worktreeConfig is true. Without extensions.worktreeConfig, Git ignores config.worktree, and so does the reader.

title: Git reader
text: Call Result repo.head() Head::Branch { name, tip }, where name is the last ref of the chain, as git symbolic-ref HEAD gives it, with tip: None for an unborn branch, or Head::Detached(id); GitReadError::Ref when HEAD names a ref outside refs/. Each call reads HEAD again, so a HEAD removed after the open gives GitReadError::Ref repo.branch_tip("main") The tip of refs/heads/main from a loose ref or packed-refs, or None when the branch does not exist repo.object_kind(&id) The type of the object: commit, tree, blob or tag repo.read_commit(&id) A GitCommit, whose id() and parents() give the ID and the raw parents in the order of the object The reader parses a loose ref and HEAD as parse_loose_ref_contents of Git does. After ref:, it drops the whitespace before and after the name. A direct ref holds a full ID, and the end of the file or whitespace must follow it. So  junk and a short ID give GitReadError::Ref. Whitespace is a space, a tab, a line feed or a carriage return, as for isspace of Git. A form feed and a vertical tab are not whitespace. GitObjectId::from_hex(format, hex) parses a full ID of 40 or 64 hexadecimal digits. It returns an error for an abbreviated ID. An ID whose format differs from the format of the repository gives GitReadError::FormatMismatch. A branch name must make a valid full ref name, refs/heads/ . A name such as bad..name gives GitReadError::InvalidBranchName. A lookup follows symbolic refs, such as refs/heads/alias that names refs/heads/main. It reads at most Limits::symbolic_depth refs, five by default, as Git’s SYMREF_MAXDEPTH does. The read of HEAD counts as one of them. So a chain of five symbolic refs is too deep, and HEAD can lead through at most three symbolic branches. A ref below refs/worktree, refs/bisect or refs/rewritten, and a pseudo ref such as FOO, is private to a worktree. The reader reads its loose file from the Git directory of the worktree. Every other loose ref comes from the common directory, also a name that Git puts in no category, such as foo/bar. Without a loose file, a ref below refs/ comes from the shared packed-refs, as in Git. A ref outside refs/ without a loose file does not exist. A name that points into another worktree, such as main-worktree/refs/heads/main, gives GitReadError::Ref. A lookup in packed-refs takes the exact name, so a symbolic ref to FOO never finds refs/heads/FOO. A ref whose path crosses a file, such as refs/heads/main/sub beside the file refs/heads/main, does not exist, as in Git. Nor does a loose ref that is a link to a folder. For both, the reader looks in no packed-refs, as Git does. A real folder at the path of a ref means only that the ref is not loose, so the reader then looks in packed-refs. The reader parses packed-refs itself, as Git does. A carriage return stays in the name, so a file with CRLF line ends finds no branch. An entry with a bad name never matches, and the other entries still resolve. A last line with no line feed, or a line that is not a record, gives GitReadError::Ref. Git refuses such a file too. The parser of gix-ref differs on each of these points. read_commit returns an error for an object that is not a commit, and the error names the actual type of the object. It recomputes the hash of the bytes that it read, and it returns GitReadError::HashMismatch when the hash differs. The loose object reader of gix does not check the hash, so the module checks it. The reader reads the parents as parse_commit_buffer of Git does. It reads the tree line and each parent line, and it reads nothing after them. So a bad author line does not stop the read. An ID in these lines may have upper-case hex digits, as in Git. A body that ends right after its tree line or its last parent line gives GitReadError::MalformedCommit, as in Git. A short parent line at the end of the body also gives that error, but Git drops such a line. So the reader never gives a commit fewer parents than its body names. Each failed read keeps its underlying error as a Cause, and std::error::Error::source returns it. The error of the operating system keeps its kind, and the error of gix keeps its type. Only the reader makes a GitCommit, because its fields are private. So a GitCommit is always a commit that the reader checked.

title: Git reader
text: The reader opens the object store with gix_odb::at_opts, with no table of replacements. So refs/replace and git replace --graft never change a result. It also ignores the file info/grafts, which Git still applies. A commit gives the parents that git --no-replace-objects cat-file commit shows, and not those that git cat-file commit shows. The reader also opens the store without multi-pack-index. gix would open each pack that the index names without a check, so a FIFO there could block it. Without the index, gix reads only the regular .idx files of the pack folder. The reader gives gix the common directory as the folder against which a relative path resolves. Without it, gix reads the current folder of the process, and the open fails when that folder has been removed.

title: Git reader
text: RepositoryConfig holds the three keys of GIT-01. The reader reads them from the repository’s own files, config in the common directory and, when extensions.worktreeConfig is true, config.worktree in the Git directory. It reads no global or system configuration, and it follows no include.path. Field Meaning object_format extensions.objectFormat, or SHA-1 when the key is absent ref_storage The raw extensions.refStorage; an opened repository has None or files hooks_path The raw core.hooksPath; the value of config.worktree wins when that file applies unread_includes True when a file has an include or includeIf section, whose target the reader did not read GIT-05 says that hooks install fails when core.hooksPath is set at any level. The reader gives only the repository levels. The hooks work must also check the global and system levels, and treat unread_includes as a possible setting.

title: Git reader
text: Limits bounds each read, and the type has no unbounded default. Limits::STANDARD gives the values below. A read that passes a limit gives GitReadError::TooLarge, SymbolicDepth, TooManyParents or Alternate. A branch name that names a folder of refs gives None, and not TooLarge. The reader itself reads HEAD, each loose ref, packed-refs, a .git file, commondir, each configuration file and each alternates file. gix parses the configuration and the gitdir: line of a .git file. The reader parses a loose ref, HEAD and packed-refs itself, as Read refs and commits says. Each read works in this way: The open uses O_NONBLOCK, so a FIFO cannot stop it. The reader checks the type on the opened file. It reads a regular file only. A FIFO, a device, a socket or a dangling link gives GitReadError::NotAFile. A folder where the reader needs a file also gives NotAFile. A folder at the path of a loose ref means only that the ref is not loose. The read takes at most the limit plus one byte. So a file that grows during the read gives TooLarge, and the reader never reads more than the limit. A symbolic link to refs/... is a symbolic ref, as Git reads it. Any other link at HEAD gives NotAFile, because Git also stops with an error on such a link. The open of HEAD uses O_NOFOLLOW, so a link that replaces HEAD after the check is not followed. The reader follows any other link at a ref. A target that is a regular file is read, and a target that is a folder makes the ref missing. The open also walks the alternates files before gix reads them, and it splits the lines as gix does. Each file counts against alternates_bytes, and all alternates together count against alternates. Git reads six nested files, at levels 0 to 5, and ignores a deeper one. The reader reads the same six files, and it returns GitReadError::Alternate for an alternate in a deeper file. Each alternate must be a folder. A line keeps its spaces, as in Git and gix. The reader returns GitReadError::Alternate for three cases that gix reads otherwise than Git: A quoted alternate path. A relative path in a nested alternates file. Git resolves it against the folder of that file, but gix resolves it against the top objects folder. A folder that appears twice, such as a cycle, a repeated line or a folder that names itself. Git skips the repeat, but gix stops with an error on a cycle. gix reads the checked files once more when it opens the object store, at its first lookup and after each miss. So before each object read, the reader checks the alternates files again. A change since the open, such as a FIFO or a new alternate, gives GitReadError::Alternate, NotAFile or TooLarge. The reader then checks each loose file of the object in the same way. A FIFO there gives NotAFile and does not block the read. A change between a check and the read of gix can still pass. Field Bound Standard config_bytes Each configuration file 1 MiB small_file_bytes HEAD, each loose ref, a .git file and commondir 4 KiB packed_refs_bytes The file packed-refs 256 MiB symbolic_depth Refs read in one lookup, HEAD included 5 commit_bytes One commit object, from its header, before the read 16 MiB parents Parents of one commit 1024 alternates_bytes Each objects/info/alternates file 64 KiB alternates Alternate object folders, over all nested alternates files 16

title: Git reader
text: gix-ref and gix-odb can also write, and Rust itself cannot forbid a call to their write methods at compile time. So the module uses three guards, by GIT-03: One module. All use of gix sits in src/git_reader.rs. Its public types are its own, so a caller of the module needs no gix type. The lint. clippy.toml lists the write paths in disallowed-methods and disallowed-types. The lint recipe of the Justfile passes -F clippy::disallowed_methods -F clippy::disallowed_types. The flag -F sets each lint to forbid, so a local #[allow] cannot lift it. The test of unchanged directories. The test git_t06 hashes the common directory, the worktree Git directory and the alternate object directory. It runs every call of the module, and then it hashes them again. The hash takes the bytes, the mode, the inode and the modified time of each entry. A folder gets a new modified time when an entry is made or removed in it. So a lock file that a writer makes and removes again changes the hash. The reader makes no ref store of gix-ref. It reads and parses each loose ref, HEAD and packed-refs itself, so the ref writers of gix-ref have no value that they could start from. The list bans each write method of gix_object::Write, gix_odb::sink and gix_odb::Sink, and the ref transaction of gix-ref. It also bans the locks of gix-lock, the persist of gix-tempfile, the multi-pack index writers and the writers of the configuration. It bans the serializers of Git formats too, such as gix_object::WriteTo::write_to and the reflog line of gix-ref. gix-odb builds gix-pack without the feature streaming-input. So the pack writers and the index writer do not exist in this build. Their entries in clippy.toml have allow-invalid = true, so that a later change of features cannot add them unbanned. gix-ref keeps its transaction of packed refs private, and only the banned file transaction reaches it. The test git_t07 in tests/git_write_lint.rs writes a small crate with one call of each banned path. It runs clippy on the crate with the flags of the recipe and the real clippy.toml. Each call must fail the lint, and a plain read must pass. Each entry with allow-invalid must name a writer that does not compile in this build. The test also requires -F, and not -D, for both lints. The test gix_is_used_only_in_the_reader_module checks the first guard. It fails when a source file other than src/git_reader.rs names a gix path, such as gix_odb::at. A probe text checks that the scan finds each form of the path. The test every_gix_writer_is_banned_or_explained reads the sources of each gix-* package of Cargo.lock. It finds each public function whose name says that it may write, such as write*, commit, persist*, create*, remove* and set_*. Each one found must match an entry of a table of the test, by its package, its file and its name: BANNED_SITES gives the path that clippy.toml bans for the function. EXPLAINED_SITES and EXPLAINED_METHODS give the reason why the function cannot write to Git, such as a setter of a parsed configuration in memory. The gossil crate can name only its six gix dependencies and the packages that they re-export, such as gix_pack through gix_odb::pack. The test computes that set from the sources. A free function of another package, such as gix_fs::symlink::create, needs a path that gossil cannot write, so it needs no entry. A method needs only a value of its type, so each method needs an entry in every package. Each table entry must also name a function that the scan finds. A trait method, such as WriteTo::write_to, is not a pub fn, so its ban is listed by hand. The scan matches names, so it is a best-effort guard and cannot be complete. The guarantees are the three guards above: All use of gix sits in one module. The disallowed lists of clippy.toml ban the write paths. git_t06 checks that the Git directories keep their bytes and metadata after a run of every call of the API.

title: Git reader
text: The module uses six gix crates, each pinned to an exact version, with the features sha1 and sha256 and no default features. Crate Version Role gix-discover 0.57.1 Parse the gitdir: line of a .git file gix-config 0.62.1 Parse the configuration files gix-ref 0.69.1 Check ref names and sort them into categories gix-odb 0.87.0 Read loose and packed objects, with alternates gix-object 0.66.1 Parse commits and recompute their hash gix-hash 0.28.1 Object IDs The crates build on Rust 1.95, the toolchain of the development host, and they need Rust 1.88 or later. Cargo.lock grows from 127 to 188 packages, so the crates add 61 packages for all targets. Some of them build only on Windows or on embedded targets. On macOS, just git-reader-packages counts 53 packages that only the six crates bring into the normal build. Cargo.lock already had six of the 53 for other uses, which are fastrand, getrandom, hashbrown, rustix, tempfile and zlib-rs. The hash features bring second major versions of sha2, digest, block-buffer, crypto-common and cpufeatures. The tests in tests/git_reader_packages.rs run the script of just git-reader-packages and check its count. They also check that the script fails when no package is added.

title: Git reader
section: Known differences from Git and follow-ups
text: The reader refuses some layouts that Git reads: an alternates file that names a folder twice alternates more than 5 levels deep a short parent line in a commit a loose ref of the form  \0junk a symbolic link with a target that is not a valid ref name a gitdir: path that ends in whitespace other than the line end Other differences: The reader ignores info/grafts, which Git still applies. gix skips a pack whose .idx is a symbolic link. The reader finds no name outside refs/ in packed-refs. Git binary-searches a packed-refs file whose header says sorted, even when its entries are out of order. The reader scans every line, so the two can give different answers for such a file. Some malformed layouts give GitReadError::Io where NotARepository would fit better. The code runs on Unix only. Known risks: A pack file cut short while gix maps it can end the process with SIGBUS. Object reads have no limit on the memory that gix allocates for them. The reader reads packed-refs again at each step of a symbolic chain. A file can change between a check by the reader and the later read by gix. Follow-ups: Add tests for behavior that is already correct, from the lists of the test reviewers.

title: Git reader
text: Open the worktree again for each registration, each locate and each bind. Keep each new gix call in src/git_reader.rs. Add each new write path of gix to clippy.toml, with a line of tests/git_write_lint.rs.

title: Bounded Fossil glob port
text: The glob module ports list parsing, matching and SQL expression construction from Fossil src/glob.c. It calls sqlite3_strglob from the selected libSQL 0.10.0 engine. The direct libsql-ffi dependency requests that exact version with default features disabled. The existing Cargo patch selects the accepted vendored provider for this dependency too. glob_create stores reusable patterns. Its glob_match method returns the first matching pattern’s one-based index, or zero. glob_multi_match scans once, using Fossil’s 100-byte temporary pattern buffer and allocating for longer patterns. Rust owns the buffers instead of calling glob_free. The list grammar uses commas and ASCII whitespace (bytes 9 through 13 and space). Single and double quotes retain commas and whitespace in a pattern. An unmatched opening quote consumes the rest of the list. Only a quote at the start of a term opens quoted parsing. There is no escape syntax. Empty quoted terms remain real empty patterns. Absent, empty and delimiter-only lists have no patterns. Lists, candidates and SQL value expressions end at the first NUL byte, as in C. glob_expr produces SQL bytes and doubles apostrophes in patterns. The value argument must be a trusted SQL expression. The function does not quote or sanitize that argument. Use a trusted column expression or parameter expression such as ?1. Bind an untrusted candidate separately through a caller-owned SQL interface. The function returns bytes and executes no SQL. After a closing quote, SQL construction skips one more byte, as the source does. For example, 'a'bc gives matching patterns a and bc, but SQL terms a and c. Do not normalize this distinction. SQL output joins terms with OR inside parentheses. A list with no patterns returns 0. A quoted empty pattern produces a real GLOB '' term. Callers supply finite Limits for list bytes, candidate bytes, pattern count and expression bytes. Reusable matching retains its candidate limit. Byte limits apply to the prefix before the first NUL. Finding that prefix scans until the first NUL or the end of the original slice. Reservations are fallible and capacity additions are checked. Typed errors retain allocation failures. The one-shot matcher returns as soon as a pattern matches. It need not inspect later terms against the pattern-count budget. SQLite owns wildcard syntax, Unicode character handling and matching recursion. These byte budgets bound accepted prefixes and allocations, but they do not bound SQLite matching CPU time or stack use. SQL execution can impose further engine limits on patterns and expressions. Matching follows SQLite GLOB rules. It is case sensitive, * can cross / and match dot-prefixed names, and backslashes are literal bytes rather than escapes. Character classes include ranges such as [a-c] and negation such as [^a]. The selected-engine controls include ? matching é, invalid UTF-8 bytes and an unmatched [ that matches nothing. Both gossil and gos accept vcs or its alias v. gossil vcs test-glob PATTERN STRING ... prints the SQL expression, parsed patterns and the indices returned by glob_match and glob_multi_match. The adapter uses fixed finite budgets of 1 MiB per list or candidate, 65,536 patterns and 16 MiB per expression. It rejects setting names beginning with @. Repository settings remain a follow-up. JSON rendering also remains a follow-up. Unix arguments retain their exact bytes. On other platforms, the adapter accepts Unicode arguments as UTF-8 and rejects arguments that cannot be represented as Unicode. It does not replace invalid characters. The historical qualification used Unix targets only. Non-Unix conversion has source review, without cross-compilation or runtime qualification.

title: Bounded Fossil glob port
text: This adaptation preserves the shared product entry and both thin executables. It changes no storage, tracking, traversal, settings or selection behavior. The 2026-11-21 focused checkpoint built both product binaries with the selected libSQL 0.10.0 engine. It passed 3 CLI tests, 9 glob integration tests and 5 filtered library units (4 glob units plus an existing global-state control). All 20 unchanged upstream Tcl assertions passed against the Rust diagnostic. The graph comparison retained all 126 nonroot packages and their complete edges/features, with one libsql-ffi 0.10.0 provider. The tested tree was a5583c3c6a73dda1a75ad1dd4c168efc06655c40, on actual parent 4250b873. It included a prospective checked-commit prerequisite rather than accepted prerequisite ancestry. PR 47 supplies typed commit and cleanup causes. Strict Rust 1.100 lint stopped at that prerequisite’s commit_checked large-error lint. The owner’s local lint fix is synchronized in the source successor, but this checkpoint does not qualify it. At the checkpoint, Cargo.toml set the version of the Gossil crate to 0.9.0, which was later released as v0.9.0. The current version of the crate is 0.17.0, and version 0.16.0 was released as v0.16.0. The libsql-ffi provider is at 0.10.0, and its version is separate from the version of the crate. Complete gates on the final frozen tree, accepted-parent checks, independent review, release and exact merged installation proof remain separate from the focused results.

title: Bounded Fossil glob port
text: evidence/glob/upstream-cases.hex contains all 20 glob.test assertion families, 100 through 119. A Tcl evaluation extracted arguments and expected output from the pinned source without executing Fossil. The cases record source expectations rather than newly observed native outcomes. Rust tests compare the adapter output with each original expectation, including CR/LF normalization. Boundary tests cover empty lists and patterns, all ASCII delimiters, unmatched and adjacent quotes, apostrophe escaping and first-match indices. They also cover NUL boundaries, 99/100-byte buffers, invalid UTF-8, Unicode, character classes, case sensitivity, slash and dotfile matching, and budgets. evidence/glob/red.log.gz records a compiled behavioral failure before adapter integration. evidence/glob/green.log.gz records the focused passing run. Historical dependency reports record package and feature identity for the earlier 0.9.30 composition. They do not establish the resolved provider or enabled features of this adaptation. run-upstream.tcl also runs the unchanged upstream test file against the Rust adapter. Its log records all 20 assertions passing. An instrumented unit-test probe received SIGKILL before tests ran. Its cause remains unresolved. The separate focused instrumented integration run passed all six tests. Those early results did not establish a full coverage gate pass. The later historical composed run in evidence/glob-provider-integration/ passes the coverage gate with all 293 changed executable lines covered. All 20 unchanged upstream Tcl assertions pass against the Rust diagnostic. Other tests cover ordinary API and conversion behavior, invalid arity, settings rejection and errors from closed stdout. Engine checks retain the selected vendored source and unchanged feature set. The accepted timeline baseline is 4250b873, released as v0.8.0. The focused glob checkpoint above does not establish final integration acceptance. Confirm the accepted checked-commit prerequisite and qualify the complete resulting tree before delivery. The composed results are observations of the Rust candidate, not a fresh native Fossil run. historical-log-packaging.json maps the two compressed historical raw logs to their original paths and records their lossless gzip packaging. The source is copyright 2011 D. Richard Hipp, and the tests are copyright 2013 D. Richard Hipp, both under the 2-Clause BSD license retained in evidence/glob/fossil-license.txt.
