title: Check-in graph paths
text: The gossil::history module finds paths and common ancestors in caller-supplied check-in rows. Use it to inspect graph behavior in memory with finite input and search limits. Its algorithms come from Fossil’s path.c and pqueue.c. On this page, “native” means those algorithms and their queue order. The caller supplies the graph and resolves its branch and time metadata. This module opens no database and grants no permission to read repository history. The broader history API remains partial. Persistence, branch management and sync remain separate work.

title: Check-in graph paths
text: Graph::new borrows a slice of Checkin metadata and indexes the supplied links. Each check-in needs a unique positive rid, branch bytes without NUL and a finite Julian-day time. A Julian day is the numeric count of days that Fossil uses for time. The caller resolves native branch defaults and missing times before construction. ParentLink supplies a parent, child and primary-parent flag for each plink row. Cherrypick supplies a source, destination and exclusion flag for each cherrypick row. Both endpoints must occur in the check-in slice. Keep the native query order of both slices of rows, with their duplicates and excluded cherrypicks. Construction keeps the row order of each direction, and it sorts only a separate index of identifiers. A new order of the rows can change which path of equal cost a search returns. The retained native capture script queries child and parent plink rows without ORDER BY. The field query_rows in the recorded fixture retains the observed order. This graph API imposes no database query order.

title: Check-in graph paths
text: Call Result and purpose Graph::new(nodes, links, cherries, limits) Validate metadata and index ordered graph rows. graph.shortest(from, to, options) Return an owned Path between two known check-ins, or Ok(None) when the search finds no path. graph.common_ancestor(me, you) Return an Ancestor with a shared pivot and a diagnostic path, or Ok(None) when the search finds no ancestor. For shortest, set these Options explicitly: Option Behavior primary_only Skip non-primary parent links. direction: Direction::Both Search backwards until the first forward step, then forwards only. direction: Direction::Forward Search from parent to child only. direction: Direction::ForwardWithCherrypicks Also permit a non-excluded cherrypick as the first edge only. hidden Keep these known identifiers traversable and charge their cost, but exclude hidden steps from bisect counts. branch_cost: 0 Charge one per node, including the starting node. branch_cost: positive Start at zero, then charge absolute time distance plus this penalty for each branch change. The starting node remains visible even when its identifier occurs in hidden. A positive branch cost must fit i32. A search with a positive branch cost can return a path with more edges than the unweighted path, because it minimizes a different cost. The native queue does not take equal costs in first-in, first-out (FIFO) order. On insertion, a heap parent with an equal cost stays in place. On removal, the queue swaps through equal costs and prefers the left child on a tie. A shortest-path search visits the child rows before the backwards rows. These rules and the order of the input rows decide each tie. common_ancestor searches backwards from both endpoints. If either endpoint is zero, it returns Ok(None). If the two endpoints are equal, known and positive, it returns a path of one element. The returned path can start at either requested endpoint, because the native order of discovery sets its orientation.

title: Check-in graph paths
text: Path.steps includes both endpoints. Each Step contains its identifier, a from_is_parent direction flag and its hidden status. Path.cost contains the native cumulative cost. For a shortest path, from_is_parent is true when the preceding step is the parent of this step. The first step has no preceding edge. Ancestor paths keep the native rewiring behavior, which can leave a direction flag false. So the flags of an ancestor path do not say whether the preceding step is the parent. Path::visible_steps counts non-hidden elements after the starting element. midpoint counts backwards from the destination, and it returns no element when the path has fewer than two visible steps. search_depth estimates the number of bisect comparisons that remain as the ceiling of log2 of the visible count. It returns zero for a count below two. These helpers describe the returned path. They do not implement a persisted bisect session or authorize access to its elements.

title: Check-in graph paths
text: There is no default Limits value. Choose every bound for the application: Field Bound checkins Number of supplied check-ins; also limits the length of hidden. links Combined number of parent and cherrypick rows, including excluded rows. branch_bytes Sum of all supplied branch byte lengths. search_nodes Allocated search records, including duplicate pending records. row_visits Adjacency rows inspected by each search, including filtered rows. The bounds limit counts and traversal, and not the total bytes on the heap. Error::Limit reports exhausted bounds. InvalidGraph reports malformed metadata, unknown identifiers or a cyclic chain of predecessors inside a search. NonFiniteCost reports an overflow in a time difference or in the cumulative cost. Allocation keeps the typed error of the failed reservation. A failed search returns no partial path. When the search finds no path, it succeeds with None. Graph validation checks the shape of the supplied data. Derived plink rows alone cannot establish provenance, private membership or complete history. A future storage adapter needs its own checks of admission and scope before it supplies rows.

title: Check-in graph paths
text: The port follows Fossil check-in 7e8ecf0ce4, the same check-in as the reference binary of the project. The sources are in src/path.c and src/pqueue.c: Native function Lines Port path_new_node src/path.c lines 106 to 138 Search::add path_shortest src/path.c lines 184 to 271 Graph::shortest path_midpoint src/path.c lines 277 to 285 Path::midpoint path_search_depth src/path.c lines 313 to 317 Path::search_depth path_common_ancestor src/path.c lines 396 to 447 Graph::common_ancestor pqueuex_rebalance src/pqueue.c lines 99 to 109 Search::add pqueuex_pop src/pqueue.c lines 131 to 146 Search::pop The caller resolves branches as branch_of_rid does in src/branch.c, lines 57 to 73, and times as mtime_of_rid does in src/descendants.c, lines 166 to 175. The record evidence/history/source-correspondence.json maps each function of path.c to its port or says why it is not ported. It also lists each line of the native source that calls a function of path.c, and the SHA256 of each cited source file. The record holds 17 lines for the three search functions and 16 lines in other files for the other functions. The fixtures under tests/fixtures/history/ hold the Fossil license and two captures, with the scripts that made them. The Fossil 2.29 reference binary made both captures over a synthetic repository: native.json holds 16 runs of test-shortest-path and 9 runs of test-ancestor-path, with their commands, outputs and parsed paths. native-queue.json holds one run of test-pqueue with five equal costs. A fresh capture with the same binary gave the same paths, pivots and queue order. Only the random identity of the scratch repository differed. The output of fossil new holds that identity and a throwaway admin password of the scratch repository. The capture script replaces the project-id, the server-id and the password with placeholders, and the field redactions of native.json records the replacement. A fresh capture with the redaction gives a file identical to the fixture. The test-shortest-path command has no option for the first-hop cherrypick direction, so Direction::ForwardWithCherrypicks has no native capture. A Rust test checks it against src/path.c lines 226 to 240. The tests in tests/history.rs replay all 25 captured cases. They also check the controls that the port adds for bounds, malformed input, cost overflow, cycles and endpoint orientation. A test checks each bound at the last value that it accepts and at the next value, which it refuses. Other tests check the midpoint and the search depth at two and four visible steps, and that rows in an unsorted order keep their order. Three unit tests in src/history.rs check the typed allocation error, the native queue order and the error for a cyclic chain of predecessors. The doc comments of Graph::shortest and Graph::common_ancestor hold two doctests. The inherited Tcl tests of the pinned check-in do not call either diagnostic, so no inherited assertion applies. These tests do not qualify Gossil repository access or the native callers in bisect, annotation, file history and timeline.

title: Gossil
text: Gossil aims to keep agent work, issues and file history together alongside Git. Fossil is a version-control system. This build exposes a Rust library for Fossil’s delta bytes, artifact parsing and local storage. The gossil command creates, applies and checks deltas between files without a version-control checkout. It also initializes an empty repository through vcs init, without creating a checkout. The source vcs open command registers or reopens one native checkout and publishes its lookup locator without selecting files. The CLI and library also select explicit path scopes and record a complete private tracked tree while the shared root stays empty. Scope assigns a tracked path to shared or owner-local private history. Shared recording remains planned. Start with a file round trip, browse the CLI reference, or use the Rust API reference. Use working with repositories to plan agent files alongside Git. It explains checkouts, stored history and the intended private and shared workflows. For an already installed development preview, try the disposable file-history walkthrough. The preview is unmerged. Read compare Gossil with Git for the planned coordination of file history, exact issue state and versioned links to code. The examples show library calls for deltas, compressed bytes, hashes and token escaping. Gest is a task and artifact tracker. The converters in the module table use its record model for tasks, projects, authors, artifacts, iterations, tags, notes, relationships, entity tags and iteration tasks. Use vcs info to show the current recorded checkout and its shared and private heads. Explicit repository and checkout selections and a complete locator are required. The source vcs timeline and vcs log commands print complete recorded ancestry as compact NDJSON. Historical revision selection remains unsupported. The library can read complete recorded ancestry through recorded_timeline, with native metadata bytes and the shared root last.

title: Gossil
text: The source add and status commands enroll exact paths and list pending or recorded paths with their stored scope. Add alone chooses neither shared nor private scope and stores no file bytes. The private recording library requires explicit private scope for every tracked path and captures all current bytes and executable modes. The source scope and commit commands require explicit repository, checkout, scope and recording metadata. Try the private recording walkthrough. Development status separates this source contract from released and installed versions.

title: Gossil
text: Try the file round trip first. Next, choose a module guide and use the generated API reference for its exact types, methods and errors.

title: Read tasks with task list and task show
text: The issue task list command prints the tasks of a project, and issue task show prints one task. Both read the private tasks that the issue ticket writer stored. A task ID is the 32-letter Gest ID of the task, with each letter from k to z. The text output of both commands is provisional. It is plain and stable text with no color. It is not the styled table of Gest, and a later build can change it. The JSON output follows Gest. The code is in src/product/issue_read.rs. The parsers, the selection and the printers are pure functions. The two handlers take a repository that the caller opened. The commands gos i task list and gos i task show open the repository of the checkout and call the handlers, as the CLI reference says. task list lists the tasks of the project bound to the checkout. Before gos i init binds a project, both commands exit with 78.

title: Read tasks with task list and task show
text: task list accepts these options: -a or --all shows tasks in every status. Without it, the list leaves out each task that is done or cancelled. -s STATUS or --status STATUS keeps only the tasks in that status. As in Gest, the default list leaves out a done task also when --status done asks for it. To list the done tasks, use --all --status done. -j or --json prints JSON. task show takes one task ID or prefix, and -j or --json. Both commands accept the global --no-color and --no-pager. The two options change nothing, because the output has no color and no pager. Short options can share one argument, as in -aj, and a value can follow its option, as in -sdone or --status=done. -s= gives an empty value, which is not a valid status. As in the Rust parser Clap, a value in its own argument cannot start with -, unless it is - alone. So -s -x has a missing value. Each option can appear only once, and so can --no-color and --no-pager. Only -v can repeat, because the parser counts it. As in Clap, the parser reports a repeated option at the letter that repeats it, also when the first copy is in an earlier argument. It does so before it reads a later unknown letter. So -aah and -a -ax both fail with the argument '--all' cannot be used more than once. The parser also accepts the other options of the Gest pin, which is the Gest commit eaf821b that this build follows. This build does not support those options, so the command then exits with 69: task list: --assigned-to, --limit, -t or --tag, -q or --quiet, -r or --raw, and -v or --verbose task show: -q or --quiet, -r or --raw, and -v or --verbose The parser fails, with exit status 2, on each of these arguments: an unknown option, a repeated option, a missing value, or a value given to an option that takes none an invalid status, or a --limit value that is not a whole number an extra argument, or no ID for task show an argument that is not UTF-8 The parser checks every argument before the command refuses an unsupported option. So --limit x exits with 2, and --limit 5 exits with 69.

title: Read tasks with task list and task show
section: What task list and task show check
text: task list reads each typed task row of the repository with its ticket ID and artifact name. It replays no artifact, so its cost grows with the count of tasks and not with the rest of the repository. It does not compare the rows with the artifacts. gos v verify does. task show reads only the task rows whose ID starts with the prefix. Then it proves the one task, as gos v verify --issue does. It replays the artifact of the task, compares the rows of the task with that replay, and prints the task from its artifact. Both commands first run the checks of each command, which the native storage guide lists.

title: Read tasks with task list and task show
text: The newest created_at comes first, as in Gest. When two tasks have the same created_at, the task that was stored later comes first. The caller can give a project ID, and then the list keeps only the tasks of that project.

title: Read tasks with task list and task show
text: task show finds a task as Gest resolve_id does: The prefix must have 1 to 32 letters, each from k to z. So an uppercase letter is invalid, and the command exits with 64. The command searches the tasks whose status is not done or cancelled. If exactly one task ID starts with the prefix, that task is the result. If none of those matches, the command searches every task. The search covers the tasks of every project. It does not match a project ID. The command exits with 66 when the prefix matches no task, or when the first search with a match finds more than one task. The messages are Gest’s: not found: id prefix 'lz' ambiguous id prefix 'lq': matches 2 entities Id prefix must contain only characters k-z, found 'L' The command exits with 74 when open, its checks or the proof of the task refuse the repository, or when the command cannot write the output. Both commands take the write lock of the repository, as every issue command does. A read can wait for that lock past its timeout and refuse with database is locked. Then the command opens the repository again and tries once more. After a second refusal, it exits with 74. A commit of another process between two commands needs no retry, because each command checks what it reads in its own transaction.

title: Read tasks with task list and task show
text: task list prints one line for each task. Two spaces separate the four fields of the line: the short ID, which is the first 8 letters of the task ID the status, padded to 11 characters the priority, as P and its number, padded to 4 characters the title A missing priority prints --. An empty list prints nothing. lqsppppp in-progress P1 Task p lqrooooo open P1 Task o lmommmmm open P1 Task m task show prints one labelled line for each stored field, then the description. It indents each line of the description by four spaces: id lqrooooooooooooooooooooooooooooo title Task o status open priority 1 project kkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkk assigned to none metadata {} created at 2026-11-18T12:00:03Z updated at 2026-11-18T12:00:03Z resolved at none ticket 0000000000000000000000000000000000000004 artifact   description First line of the description The ticket line gives the K card, and the artifact line gives the native name of the creation artifact. A missing value prints none. The metadata is compact JSON. Times are RFC 3339 in UTC, as the JSON writes them. A control character in a title prints as a Rust escape, such as \t, so that one field cannot break the layout. The description keeps its line breaks and escapes each other control character.

title: Read tasks with task list and task show
text: The JSON matches Gest’s envelopes, pretty-printed, with a final newline. task list --json prints an array, and an empty list prints []. Each object has the eleven fields of the Gest task model. Their order is assigned_to, created_at, description, id, metadata, priority, project_id, resolved_at, status, title and updated_at. Then come relationships and tags. task show --json prints one object, with notes before relationships, as Gest does. This build stores no notes, relationships or tags. So the three lists are always empty, as Gest prints them for a task without any. The status in-progress prints as inprogress, because Gest’s serializer spells it that way. A task in this build has no field that Gest’s JSON lacks. So every field matches, as long as Gest’s own output is the reference.

title: Read tasks with task list and task show
text: tests/issue_read_cli.rs runs the two commands through both executables and both group names. It builds a checkout with gos v init, gos v open and gos i init, and stores four tasks through the library, one of them in another project. A task needs its project, so the test stores each project first. It checks the output of each form, each exit status from 2 to 78, the help forms and a closed stdout. After each read it checks that no byte of the repository changed. tests/issue_task_cli.rs also reads back the tasks that gos i task create stores, through both commands in each form. It compares the listed IDs with the stored IDs as a set. A further test in that file holds the write lock from another connection for 7 seconds. A task list and a task show that start meanwhile both exit with 0 and print the task. The first attempt of each waits the 5-second busy timeout and refuses, and the second attempt gets the lock. Without the retry, both commands exit with 74. The test then runs a task create and a task list at the same time, and both exit with 0. The unit controls in tests/support/product_issue_read.rs check the parsers, the lookup, the selection and the exact bytes of each printer. Further controls build a catalog 6 repository through the library, with a project and four tasks, two of them after a private check-in. Then they run both handlers and check: the order, the default filter, --all, --status and the project filter the JSON, parsed back and compared with the stored fields a unique prefix, a missing one, an ambiguous one and an invalid one a failed write, which exits with 74 a task row that another connection changes, which the list prints and the show refuses with 74 before any output. A new open admits the repository, and verify refuses it. just issue-read-oracle compares the JSON with a reference gest. It creates two tasks with gest, stores the same values in a Gossil repository and requires equal bytes from task show --json, task list --json and task list --all --json. It runs the gest that GOSSIL_GEST_REFERENCE names, or else the gest on the path. The installed gest 0.6.0 is a fork, not the Gest pin eaf821b, so a pass checks that build only. Without a gest, the recipe exits with 5, which means not-run and not a pass.

title: Read tasks with task list and task show
text: Keep the selection and the lookup equal to Gest repo::task::all and resolve_id. Treat the text output as provisional, and parse the JSON in scripts.

title: Store a private issue ticket
text: The issue ticket writer stores one Gest task or project in a native repository, so that stock Fossil 2.29 can read the ticket, check it and rebuild it. A ticket is the Fossil record of a piece of work. Gossil writes each Gest task and project as a ticket, and the task ticket and Gest ticket emitters make its creation artifact. A creation artifact is the first and only artifact of a ticket in this build. The writer is a library method of LocalOwnerRepository in src/storage/issue_ticket.rs. A second method, init_private_project, writes a project and binds it to the registered checkout. The command gos i init calls that method, and gos i task create calls create_private_issue for a task in the bound project. The repository must be at catalog 6, the newest catalog of Gossil storage.

title: Store a private issue ticket
text: Emit the creation artifact first, with task_creation_bytes or project_creation_bytes. Then give the bytes to the writer, with explicit limits: use gossil::storage::{IssueLimits, PathScope, PrivateIssueRequest}; let limits = IssueLimits { admission, sql_rows: 100_000, sql_bytes: 64 << 20 }; let request = PrivateIssueRequest { artifact: &bytes, scope: PathScope::Private }; let stored = owner.create_private_issue(request, limits).await?; let read = owner.read_private_issue(&stored.ticket_id, limits).await?; assert_eq!(read.record, stored.record); admission holds the content and parser limits that the whole call shares. sql_rows and sql_bytes limit the rows and bytes that the SQL queries of one call can return. The result names the ticket ID, which is the K card, and the native name of the artifact. It also holds the validated TaskValues or ProjectValues. read_private_issue runs the checks of each command, which the native storage guide lists. Then it reads the artifact that the tkt- tag of the ticket ID names, parses it and returns its record. It compares no row and writes nothing. create_private_issue runs the same checks before its write and again after it, in the same transaction and under the same limits. It parses its artifact and checks that it is one canonical creation. It checks through an index that no row holds its ticket ID, tag, artifact or Gest ID. A task also needs a project that the repository holds and that is not archived. Each check uses an index, so the cost of a write does not grow with the count of issues.

title: Store a private issue ticket
section: Bind a project to a checkout
text: init_private_project stores one project creation and binds it to the registered checkout, in one exclusive transaction: use gossil::storage::ProjectInitRequest; let request = ProjectInitRequest { artifact: &bytes, checkout_id: "work" }; let stored = owner.init_private_project(request, limits).await?; let project = owner.bound_project("work", limits).await?; assert!(project.is_some()); The method writes the rows that create_private_issue writes for a project, as the section rows that one write adds lists them. It also writes two binding rows: g_project_binding gets the checkout ID, the Gest ID of the project and the exact root of the checkout. g_checkout_project gets the checkout ID and the Gest ID of the project. Like create_private_issue, the method runs the checks of each command before and after its write. Before it changes anything, it refuses an artifact that is not one project creation, a checkout that is not registered and a checkout that already has a project. It also refuses a repository that already holds a project ticket, for example one that create_private_issue wrote. The refusal for these cases is issue init needs one project creation, a registered checkout with no bound project, and a repository with no project; binding an existing project is not available in this build. A failure before the commit leaves every byte of the repository files unchanged. bound_project returns the Gest ID of the project bound to a checkout, or None when the checkout has no binding. It runs the checks of each command first, and it writes nothing. bound_project does not use the SQL limits in limits.

title: Store a private issue ticket
text: list_private_issues returns every task and project of the repository, in the order of the receipts that stored them: let issues = owner.list_private_issues(limits).await?; for issue in &issues { println!("{} {}", issue.ticket_id, issue.native_name); } The call runs the checks of each command first. Then it reads each combined typed row with its ticket ID and artifact name. It replays no artifact, so it passes under a parser entry ceiling of one. It writes nothing. An empty repository gives an empty list. The SQL row ceiling of IssueLimits bounds the count of issues, and the parser input ceiling bounds the width of one row. The cost of the list grows with the count of issues, and not with the rest of the repository. The list does not compare the typed rows with the artifacts. gos v verify does. The issue task list handler reads the tasks through this call. The issue task show handler does not use it. It finds one task with find_task and proves it with verify_issue. The issue read guide gives the output of both commands.

title: Store a private issue ticket
section: How the full proof checks issues
text: The full proof of gos v verify finds each issue from its tkt- tag, parses its artifact again and derives every row from it. The ticket, ticketchng, g_gest_tasks and g_gest_projects tables must hold exactly the derived rows. The event, tagxref, tag, blob, private, leaf, unclustered and rcvfrom tables must hold exactly the rows of the check-ins and of the issues, with nothing else. The unsent table may hold any subset of the rows that replay gives, because a stock fossil push or fossil sync that sends nothing deletes rows from it. If any of these tables holds another row, for example a changed or extra row, the full proof refuses the repository. Issues and private check-ins can come in any order in one repository. Each check-in and each issue owns one receipt, and the receipts after the root’s have no gaps. Tags above the 12 built-in tags take their IDs in the order of the receipts that created them. So the full proof looks up the private branch tag by name. A Gest ID names one task or one project. The full proof refuses a project that reuses the Gest ID of a task, and a second ticket with the same ticket ID. The checkout fingerprint names a receipt. Registration takes the newest receipt, so when an issue comes before registration, the fingerprint names the receipt of that issue. After the first check-in, the fingerprint must name the receipt of the selected check-in, and open refuses an older fingerprint.

title: Store a private issue ticket
text: LocalOwnerRepository::verify_issue proves one task or project from its own rows, and gos v verify --issue ID runs it. It first finds the one ticket whose gest_id holds the ID. The proof of one issue checks only a subset of the repository. It proves the rows that belong to the issue and that an index reaches. The rows are its artifact, ticket, change row, event, tag, tag row, private mark, typed row and, for a task, its project. It does not claim that no other row in the repository names the issue. Only the full proof, gos v verify without --issue, makes that claim. It then checks that each table that the full proof keeps empty in every repository has no row, for example delta, cherrypick, g_gest_notes and g_gest_relationships. The check takes one fixed query per table. A row in one of these tables makes the proof refuse with unsupported nonempty catalog6 table: and the name of the table. A repository with no checkout must also keep unsent, filename, mlink, plink, g_path_scope, g_project_binding and g_checkout_project empty. The proof does not check those seven whole tables. It refuses only an unsent, mlink or plink row that names the issue, as the next paragraphs say, and only the full proof refuses every other row there. The tkt-K tag must then have one tagxref row. The RID of that row must name a private blob with a local receive record. The proof does not look for another blob with the same receipt, because no index reaches such a blob. The full proof refuses a shared receipt. No row of the unsent, unclustered, leaf, phantom, orphan or backlink table may name that blob. The same holds for an attachment row whose target is K, and for a g_public_receipt row with the hash of the blob. No mlink row may have the blob as its mid, fid or pid, and no plink row may have it as its pid or cid. No index reaches mlink.pmid or plink.baseid, so the proof does not check them. The proof replays the one artifact, which must be a canonical creation with this K. The event, tagxref, ticket and ticketchng rows of the issue must equal the replay. So must its typed row in the combined scope. The typed table of the other kind must hold no combined row with the Gest ID of the issue. For a task, the proof checks only that a combined project row with its project ID exists. When none exists, it refuses with a stored task names a project that the repository does not hold. The full proof admits such a task. The writer refuses it, so only a change outside Gossil can make one. The proof replays no other artifact. It reads the rows of this issue by an index or a primary key, except for the one lookup of the ticket by its Gest ID, which scans the ticket table. So apart from that lookup, the cost of the proof does not grow with the repository. The proof does not see a row that no index of the issue reaches, for example an unrelated tag or a ticket row without an artifact. It does not see a typed row in another scope either. Only the full proof, gos v verify without --issue, refuses those rows.

title: Store a private issue ticket
text: The writer adds these rows in one exclusive transaction: rcvfrom gets one local receipt, with uid 0, a NULL nonce and a NULL IP address. blob gets the artifact, with rcvid set to that receipt, and private marks it. tag gets tkt-K with the next free tagid, and tagxref gets (tagid, 1, rid, rid, NULL, mtime, rid). ticket and ticketchng get the decoded J fields as text, as Fossil ticket_insert writes them. event gets one row of type t. Its comment is New ticket [K16|K10]  title ., where K16 and K10 are the first 16 and 10 characters of K. The title is HTML-escaped, and a project has no title, so its comment holds   . g_gest_tasks or g_gest_projects gets the typed row, with the scope key combined. The writer adds no unclustered row, no unsent row and no backlink row. Stock Fossil writes the same rows for a private ticket, except a modreq row for moderation, which Gossil does not write. The three local audit tables transactions, transaction_events and g_command_audit stay empty. Tag IDs above 12 follow the order of the writes. When a ticket comes before the first check-in, that ticket takes tagid 13, and the first check-in gives its branch tag the next free number. When the first check-in comes before the first ticket, its branch tag takes 13, and the first ticket takes 14.

title: Store a private issue ticket
text: The writer accepts one complete task or project creation for each ticket ID. It refuses each other shape as not supported in this build, and the refusal leaves every table unchanged: a second artifact for a ticket ID that the repository holds a task whose Gest ID a project holds, or a project whose Gest ID a task holds a change to a ticket, a ticket attachment or an artifact that is not a ticket an artifact that the emitter does not write again byte for byte, for example one with an unknown field a J value that contains [, because Gossil has no port of the Markdown backlinks of Fossil a request with a scope other than private

title: Store a private issue ticket
text: Issues are private only. A write can fail and roll back after its checks passed. The next command runs its checks again in its own transaction, so a failed write does not lock out the stored tickets. Open and each command accept the binding tables g_project_binding and g_checkout_project in two states only. In the first, both tables are empty. In the second, each table holds the one row that init_private_project writes. Both rows then name the registered checkout and the Gest ID of one project that is not archived. The row of g_project_binding also holds the exact root of the checkout, and each ID must be text. Open refuses every other state with unsupported project binding state, and so does each command. In a repository without a checkout registration, open refuses every binding row. The tables g_identity and g_contributor stay empty, and the full proof refuses a row in either of them. The writer writes no audit row and no undo history. init_private_project does not bind a project that the repository already holds. The writer writes no selectors, tags of Gest or links. The scope key is the literal combined, and not the full key of the specification, because the full key needs selectors.

title: Store a private issue ticket
section: How many issues a repository holds
text: No command reads the whole repository, so no count of issues makes a write refuse. task create, status and commit each read only the rows that they need, by an index. task show finds its ticket by a scan of the ticket table, since no index holds the Gest ID, and then replays only its one artifact. task list reads every typed row, and gos v verify replays every artifact, so their cost grows with the count of issues. The scan of task show is cheap, as the times below show. just issue-capacity stores 5,000 tasks in a release build and times each command at 100, 1,000 and 5,000 tasks. One run on macOS, with 8 CPUs and load averages of about 9 before and 7 after, gave these times in milliseconds: Tasks create list show status commit verify 100 15 15 15 13 17 101 1,000 15 23 16 13 17 860 5,000 15 68 16 13 19 4,267 The times of create, show, status and commit stay flat. The times of list and verify grow with the count of tasks. gos i task create refuses a task artifact of more than 65,536 bytes.

title: Store a private issue ticket
text: tests/issue_ticket.rs checks a task and a project end to end (GEST-T01). It also checks the metadata, priority and status values that one creation can hold (part of GEST-T02), and each refused shape. The unit controls in tests/support/storage_issue_ticket.rs inject a failure after each write step. They check that every byte of the repository files stays the same (GEST-T08). They also check that the full proof refuses a changed or extra row in each admitted table, for example a tagxref row with no RID. They check too that the full proof refuses a project that reuses the Gest ID of a task, while open and the read of the project admit it. For each changed row, the ticket reader, the list and the next write refuse only a change to a fact that each one reads. For example, the reader refuses a second artifact under the tag, and the write refuses a missing project row. A new open admits each change, because none is a fact that open reads. No case changes a byte of the repository files. Each of the 29 cases of a changed row also runs the proof of one issue on the task and on the project. It checks the exact result of each proof. In 22 of the cases, at least one of the two proofs refuses. In the other 7 cases, both proofs admit the change and only the full proof refuses it. Those 7 cases add a row that no index of the issue reaches. Examples are an unrelated tag, a second event of the ticket and a change row of the artifact under another ticket. One of the 7 cases adds a second typed row in another scope. In the case of an artifact whose K is not the K of its tag, the proof of the K of the tag also refuses, with stored issue rows differ from the ticket artifact. the_proof_has_no_total_ceiling stores a project and two tasks. It sets total content ceilings of 64 bytes and a parser ceiling of 20 entries, far below what the whole repository needs. Under them verify passes and counts 0 check-ins and 3 issues. A parser input ceiling of 64 bytes makes verify refuse. Under the same small ceilings, verify_issue proves a task and a project, and find_issue finds each of them by a prefix. find_issue refuses the prefixes "", "a" and 33 letters with invalid issue ID prefix. No step changes a byte. Most cases of the_issue_proof_refuses_each_row_that_names_its_artifact add one row that names the task, by its artifact or by its Gest ID. A phantom, orphan, delta, cherrypick, g_gest_notes or g_gest_relationships row makes the proof of the task refuse with the message of that nonempty table. An mlink row with the artifact as its mid, fid or pid makes it refuse with stored issue rows differ from the ticket artifact. So does a plink row with the artifact as its pid or cid. So do a g_public_receipt row with the hash of the artifact and a combined project row with the Gest ID of the task. One more case deletes the ticket row of the task, which gives the same refusal. The test also checks the exact refusal of the full proof for each case. Other tamper tests of check-ins, tracking, scopes and the timeline take the exact refusal of the full proof from tests/fixtures/tamper-refusals.tsv. Each line of that table holds a tamper statement, a tab and the first line of the refusal. assert_refusal in tests/support/proof.rs fails on a statement that the table does not hold, or on a different message. only_the_full_proof_refuses_rows_that_no_index_reaches adds each of these in turn: a second blob under the receipt of the task an mlink row whose pmid is the task artifact a plink row whose baseid is the task artifact The proof of the task admits each, and verify refuses each. a_task_needs_its_project checks that the writer refuses a task whose project the repository does not hold, or holds archived, and changes no byte. Then it deletes the typed row of the project. The proof of the task and verify_issue both refuse the task with the message of a missing project. verify_issue also refuses an ID that no ticket holds. The unit test a_per_artifact_parser_ledger_does_not_accumulate in src/storage/repository.rs checks that a per-artifact parser ledger keeps its whole allowance after each parse, and still refuses one artifact over its ceiling. tests/vcs_verify_cli.rs checks gos v verify in all four forms. It checks the exact summary verified: 1 check-ins, 4 issues, 15 tables compared. It proves one task by its full ID and by a prefix, and the project by a prefix. It checks the usage line and the status of a usage error. It also checks the statuses of an invalid, missing or ambiguous prefix, and the exact count of an ambiguous prefix. A changed typed row makes both forms exit with status 74 and the fixed message. Open admits the row, so the proof itself refuses it. open_refuses_each_fact_that_it_reads changes one fact that open reads in each case. The cases are a wrong catalog marker, a wrong fingerprint, a missing server-code or project-code config row, a missing owner row, a wrong checkout count and lost Gossil tables. verify and status each refuse at open, before their own work, and print the same message, and neither changes a byte. Lost tables give exit 78 to both. Lost tables also make gos i task list and gos i task show exit with 78 and the same message. verify_counts_no_check_in_and_refuses_an_older_catalog checks a repository without a commit. It prints verified: 0 check-ins, 3 issues, 15 tables compared. With stdout closed, the command exits with 1 and prints gossil: unable to write the summary: . A repository at catalog 4 makes both forms exit with 78 and print three lines. No case changes a byte of the repository. Further unit controls cover init_private_project. A failure injected after each write step, the binding step included, leaves every byte unchanged and the checkout unbound. The method refuses a task, an unknown checkout, a bound checkout, a repository that holds an unbound project and a repository without a registration. Open refuses each changed, missing or extra binding row, a binding to a task or to an archived project, and a value that is not text. Before each change, the list call returns all three issues of the bound repository. After the change, the reader of the binding, the list call and a new open each refuse with unsupported project binding state. tests/issue_init_cli.rs checks the command gos i init in all four forms, its second run, its refusals and the vcs commands before and after it. tests/issue_task_cli.rs checks gos i task create in the same way, and reads each stored task back with read_private_issue. It also creates a task in each of the four forms. Then it checks that gos i task list --json lists all four, and that gos i task show --json shows the stored ID, title and priority of each. It runs two task create commands at the same time, four times, and requires that both exit with 0. A further test in tests/issue_task_cli.rs holds the write lock for 7 seconds. A task list and a task show that start meanwhile retry and exit with 0. Then the test runs a task create beside a task list. The unit tests of src/product/issue_task.rs inject a failure after each write step of a new task. Then they check that every byte of the repository stays unchanged (GEST-T08). A further unit test there opens a second owner, and then the first owner commits. The second owner needs no second open. task create writes its task, and gos i init finds the project of the first owner. When no project is bound and the write of an init refuses, the init exits with 74 and the message of the write, and stores no project. A unit control in src/storage/repository/recorded_history.rs measures the charge of the checks of each command at 3, 6 and 12 issues, and checks that it stays the same. Further unit controls there check that repeated owner checks charge the schema once per admission. They also check that the ledger charges exactly the TEXT and BLOB bytes of a result. A unit control in src/storage/content.rs checks that the ledger charges a surface once per admission, and later only its growth. It also checks that the ledger charges and holds nothing for a refused reservation. tests/issue_capacity.rs uses the ceilings of the CLI. Its ordinary test stores 300 tasks, then runs task create, task list, task show, status, commit and verify, and checks the output of each. The ignored test stores 5,000 tasks and prints the time of each command at 100, 1,000 and 5,000 tasks. just issue-capacity runs the ignored test in a release build. A unit control lists two tasks and two projects in receipt order under a parser entry ceiling of one, and checks that the list changes no row. It finds the least SQL row ceiling under which the list passes, and checks that one more task makes the list refuse under that ceiling. It also checks that find_task refuses an empty prefix, a prefix of 33 letters and a prefix outside the letters k to z, with invalid issue ID prefix. A further control stores the ID of each task as a blob. A prefix still matches such an ID, and then find_task refuses the task with a stored typed row does not hold a valid task or project and changes no row of any table. In each of its three orders, the CAT-T07 subset below also lists the issues after each step. The CAT-T07 subset in tests/issue_ticket.rs writes issues and check-ins in three orders. In the first, an issue comes before the checkout is registered. In the second, issues come before the first check-in, and in the third, issues come after check-ins. After each step, a new open admits the repository, and the commands status, add, commit and timeline work. With check-ins between the issues, the full proof still refuses a changed issue, tag or receipt row, for example swapped tag IDs or swapped receipts. Open admits each change but one, the swapped receipt of the selected check-in, because that is the only fact among them that open reads. A further test checks which receipt the fingerprint names before and after the first check-in. just issue-ticket-interop runs the stock Fossil check with the pinned Fossil 2.29 at 7e8ecf0ce4. It writes a task and a project, then requires these results of stock Fossil: fossil test-integrity --parse reports 0 errors. fossil ticket show returns each J value byte for byte. fossil test-ticket-rebuild all and fossil rebuild each write the same ticket, change, event, tag, private, unclustered, unsent and backlink rows as Gossil. It then writes check-ins with gos and an issue between them. On that repository, stock Fossil must report 0 errors from fossil test-integrity --parse. It must list both check-ins and the new ticket in fossil timeline, and show the ticket in fossil ticket show. just catalog-interop runs this check too. Last, the recipe runs the ignored test stock_fossil_reads_a_repository_after_issue_init in tests/issue_init_cli.rs. The test runs gos v init, gos v open, gos i init, gos i task create, one commit and a second gos i task create. Stock Fossil must then report 0 errors from fossil test-integrity --parse, and fossil ticket show must show the private project and both tasks. The comparison counts event times in whole milliseconds. Fossil formats event.mtime with its own conversion, which adds noise after the ninth decimal place of the Julian day. The comment bytes must be equal. If the reference is absent, the recipe exits 5, which means not-run and not a pass.

title: Store a private issue ticket
text: Validate a record with its converter, emit its creation artifact, and store it with create_private_issue. Bind a project to a checkout only with init_private_project. Run just issue-ticket-interop after a change to the writer, and report not-run apart from a pass.

title: Track issues beside your files
text: Gossil keeps the history of your files and the issues of your project in one repository file. This page is for a reader who has built gos from source and wants to see the issue commands work. It walks through one session from an empty directory to tasks and check-ins in the same repository. Then it reads that repository with stock Fossil, the Fossil 2.29 program that Gossil follows. The issue commands follow Gest, a task tracker. A Gest project holds tasks, and each task has a title, a status, a priority and a description. Gossil stores each task as a Fossil ticket, a record that stock Fossil can read. The output below is real output of this build. The only edit shortens the paths to start with ~/demo. The IDs, hashes and times differ in each run. The test tests/issue_demo.rs runs the same steps and checks each output.

title: Track issues beside your files
section: Make a repository and record a file
text: Make the repository, then open a checkout in an empty directory. A checkout is a directory whose files the repository tracks: $ mkdir -p ~/demo/work $ gos v init ~/demo/demo.gossil project-id: e11a10948be0b79e1159f51d7b89693bab4186fb server-id: 1f07f5bb7fcdd26f943fb75ffea4c227d9518a34 admin-user: me (initial remote-access password is "LXaR3stVbQ") $ cd ~/demo/work $ gos v open --repository ~/demo/demo.gossil --checkout work --root ~/demo/work Opened checkout work at ~/demo/work (repository e11a10948be0b79e1159f51d7b89693bab4186fb, head ea969fa75ea66defa9a7f57d31cec800b18c45437af074fc4789d169343b2e30) Add a file, give it the private scope and record it. Private history stays in this repository and is not shared. The date of a check-in must come after the date of the empty check-in that gos v init made. Otherwise gos v commit exits with status 1 and prints private manifest date must follow all parents. The dates are in UTC, and each check-in must also come after the one before it. So give a UTC date after the time of your own run, not the dates below. me is the user name that gos v init prints as admin-user, so give --user your own user name: $ echo hello > README.txt $ gos v add --repository ~/demo/demo.gossil --checkout work --path README.txt Tracked paths (A: pending addition, R: recorded): A unselected "README.txt" $ gos v scope --repository ~/demo/demo.gossil --checkout work --scope private --path README.txt Selected scopes: 1 $ gos v commit --repository ~/demo/demo.gossil --checkout work --scope private --all-tracked --user me --comment "Add the readme" --date-override 2026-11-25T14:00:00 Recorded private check-in: 4a2cc7ea4fcaf7d31b299f58c9d9058571d28842e162e1f803561b6b4290e2b7

title: Track issues beside your files
text: Run gos i init in the checkout. It makes one Gest project and binds it to the checkout. The later issue commands then use the project of the checkout: $ gos i init ✓ initialized project szxwzssq root ~/demo/work The short ID szxwzssq is the first 8 letters of the project ID.

title: Track issues beside your files
text: gos i task create TITLE stores one private task. The second task below has a description, a priority and the status done. With --json, the command prints the task as Gest prints it: $ gos i task create "Write the guide" ✓ created task lpswtmum title Write the guide $ gos i task create "Fix the parser" --description "The parser drops the last line." --priority high --status done ✓ created task zsoopoor title Fix the parser $ gos i task create "Check stock Fossil" --json { "assigned_to": null, "created_at": "2026-11-25T12:21:52.339358Z", "description": "", "id": "uwllrqzlnvkwuxlxworwvnqmvryzlmyt", "metadata": {}, "priority": null, "project_id": "szxwzssqvlryqrtrztyotnrwspvtwurz", "resolved_at": null, "status": "open", "title": "Check stock Fossil", "updated_at": "2026-11-25T12:21:52.339358Z", "notes": [], "relationships": [], "tags": [] } Gossil stores the priority high as the number 1. The task create section of the CLI reference gives every option.

title: Track issues beside your files
text: gos i task list prints the tasks of the project, the newest first. It leaves out each task that is done or cancelled. With --all, it shows them too: $ gos i task list uwllrqzl open -- Check stock Fossil lpswtmum open -- Write the guide $ gos i task list --all uwllrqzl open -- Check stock Fossil zsoopoor done P1 Fix the parser lpswtmum open -- Write the guide Each line gives the short ID, the status, the priority and the title. -- means that the task has no priority. With --json, the command prints a list of the tasks: $ gos i task list --json [ { "assigned_to": null, "created_at": "2026-11-25T12:21:52.339358Z", "description": "", "id": "uwllrqzlnvkwuxlxworwvnqmvryzlmyt", "metadata": {}, "priority": null, "project_id": "szxwzssqvlryqrtrztyotnrwspvtwurz", "resolved_at": null, "status": "open", "title": "Check stock Fossil", "updated_at": "2026-11-25T12:21:52.339358Z", "relationships": [], "tags": [] }, { "assigned_to": null, "created_at": "2026-11-25T12:21:50.901739Z", "description": "", "id": "lpswtmumnntmtkmlzwwklsulwswylvqz", "metadata": {}, "priority": null, "project_id": "szxwzssqvlryqrtrztyotnrwspvtwurz", "resolved_at": null, "status": "open", "title": "Write the guide", "updated_at": "2026-11-25T12:21:50.901739Z", "relationships": [], "tags": [] } ] The JSON of a task is the same in create, list and show. Only the list leaves out the empty notes field, as Gest does.

title: Track issues beside your files
text: gos i task show ID prints one task. The ID can be a prefix of the task ID, when no other task starts with it. Here zs names the done task. Use a prefix of an ID from your own run: $ gos i task show zs id zsoopoorkotyulsvmpsmzwkyurrvnlzz title Fix the parser status done priority 1 project szxwzssqvlryqrtrztyotnrwspvtwurz assigned to none metadata {} created at 2026-11-25T12:21:51.577902Z updated at 2026-11-25T12:21:51.577902Z resolved at 2026-11-25T12:21:51.577902Z ticket e3faa7a638bcd39e3b0cb02489be6026b357236b artifact 675b687bb4d07b122f8c037e617747ae515579f7474357f63524c1c7a4f98d41 description The parser drops the last line. The ticket line gives the ID of the Fossil ticket that holds the task. The --json form prints the same fields as create. The issue read guide explains each field and the search by prefix.

title: Track issues beside your files
section: Record more files after the tasks
text: The file commands work as before after you create tasks. Record a second file, then read the history and the tracked files: $ echo notes > NOTES.txt $ gos v add --repository ~/demo/demo.gossil --checkout work --path NOTES.txt Tracked paths (A: pending addition, R: recorded): A unselected "NOTES.txt" R private "README.txt" $ gos v scope --repository ~/demo/demo.gossil --checkout work --scope private --path NOTES.txt Selected scopes: 1 $ gos v commit --repository ~/demo/demo.gossil --checkout work --scope private --all-tracked --user me --comment "Add the notes" --date-override 2026-11-25T14:05:00 Recorded private check-in: a3e4de678d864919a194b6b46a139ac47c41637fb42e26caac2d751c026697db $ gos v timeline --repository ~/demo/demo.gossil --checkout work {"hash":"a3e4de678d864919a194b6b46a139ac47c41637fb42e26caac2d751c026697db","date":"2026-11-25T14:05:00","actor":"me","comment":"Add the notes","private":true} {"hash":"4a2cc7ea4fcaf7d31b299f58c9d9058571d28842e162e1f803561b6b4290e2b7","date":"2026-11-25T14:00:00","actor":"me","comment":"Add the readme","private":true} {"hash":"ea969fa75ea66defa9a7f57d31cec800b18c45437af074fc4789d169343b2e30","date":"2026-11-25T12:21:48.289","actor":"me","comment":"initial empty check-in","private":false} $ gos v status --repository ~/demo/demo.gossil --checkout work Tracked paths (A: pending addition, R: recorded): R private "NOTES.txt" R private "README.txt" gos v timeline lists the check-ins only, and not the tasks.

title: Track issues beside your files
text: Each command of the sections above checks only what it reads and writes. gos v verify checks the whole repository. It replays every check-in and every issue, compares each table with that replay and changes nothing. With --issue ID, it checks only the rows of one task or project. The verify section of the CLI reference gives both forms and their exit statuses: $ gos v verify --repository ~/demo/demo.gossil verified: 2 check-ins, 4 issues, 15 tables compared $ gos v verify --repository ~/demo/demo.gossil --issue zs verified issue zsoopoorkotyulsvmpsmzwkyurrvnlzz: ticket e3faa7a638bcd39e3b0cb02489be6026b357236b The 2 check-ins are the two private check-ins. The count leaves out the empty check-in of gos v init. The 4 issues are the project and the three tasks.

title: Track issues beside your files
section: Read the repository with stock Fossil
text: Stock Fossil reads the same repository file. fossil test-integrity checks every stored artifact. It finds the 3 check-ins and 4 tickets, which are the project and the three tasks: $ fossil test-integrity --parse -R ~/demo/demo.gossil all 9 blobs checked: 0 errors 0 control artifacts failed to parse 7 total control artifacts 3 manifests 4 tickets low-level database integrity-check: ok fossil timeline shows the check-ins and the tickets in one list: $ fossil timeline -R ~/demo/demo.gossil === 2026-11-25 === 14:05:00 [a3e4de678d] *MERGE* *UNPUBLISHED* Add the notes (user: me tags: gossil-private/1f07f5bb7fcdd26f943fb75ffea4c227d9518a34) 14:00:00 [4a2cc7ea4f] *UNPUBLISHED* Add the readme (user: me tags: gossil-private/1f07f5bb7fcdd26f943fb75ffea4c227d9518a34) 12:21:52 [72f1dbc799] *UNPUBLISHED* New ticket [9dfb5cf383] "Check stock Fossil". (user: me) 12:21:51 [675b687bb4] *UNPUBLISHED* New ticket [e3faa7a638] "Fix the parser". (user: me) 12:21:50 [55d2174fdd] *UNPUBLISHED* New ticket [09303112e3] "Write the guide". (user: me) 12:21:50 [e2239de3dd] *UNPUBLISHED* New ticket [12f8ca15f2] . (user: me) 12:21:48 [ea969fa75e] initial empty check-in (user: me tags: trunk) +++ no more data (7) +++ *UNPUBLISHED* marks private content. The second private check-in shows *MERGE*, because it names the shared root as a second parent, as the native storage guide explains. The ticket without a title is the project. fossil ticket show prints the ticket fields of each task, one row for each task and one column for each field. The command below keeps four of the columns. The --user value must be a user of the repository, such as the admin-user, or Fossil prints No such user and the name. Do not add a ticket with fossil ticket add. It crashes in the pinned Fossil: $ fossil ticket show 0 "gossil_kind='task'" --user me -R ~/demo/demo.gossil | cut -f 2,6,8,13 tkt_uuid status priority title 09303112e37e88bb29792eeda4767a6b961b0b3d "open" null "Write the guide" e3faa7a638bcd39e3b0cb02489be6026b357236b "done" 1 "Fix the parser" 9dfb5cf38352b84a4d505c81f4b41b05da412200 "open" null "Check stock Fossil" Each value is the JSON value that Gest stores, so a text value is in quotes. A stock fossil push to a clone sends no private check-in and no task, because both are private. The push also empties the list of artifacts to send. Every gos command and gos v verify still pass after that push, and after a fossil sync or fossil pull that receives nothing. A pull or sync that receives a public artifact from the clone is not supported, and gos v verify then refuses the repository. By default, a commit in a checkout of the clone has the same effect, because Fossil autosync pushes the commit back into the Gossil file. Turn off autosync in the clone, or point the clone at another remote, before you commit there.

title: Track issues beside your files
section: Rebuild a copy with stock Fossil
text: Run fossil rebuild on a copy only, and never on the repository that you use. fossil rebuild makes the tables of Fossil again from the stored artifacts. It drops each table whose name starts with g_, and Gossil keeps its own state in those tables: $ cp ~/demo/demo.gossil ~/demo/copy.gossil $ fossil rebuild ~/demo/copy.gossil 100.0% complete... $ fossil sql -R ~/demo/demo.gossil "SELECT count(*) FROM sqlite_schema WHERE name GLOB 'g_*'" 96 $ fossil sql -R ~/demo/copy.gossil "SELECT count(*) FROM sqlite_schema WHERE name GLOB 'g_*'" 0 Stock Fossil still reads the copy. fossil test-integrity reports 0 errors, and fossil timeline and fossil ticket show list the same check-ins and tasks. Only the row numbers of the tickets can change. gos v open and gos v verify refuse the copy and leave it unchanged: $ mkdir ~/demo/other $ cd ~/demo/other $ gos v open --repository ~/demo/copy.gossil --checkout work --root ~/demo/other this repository has lost its Gossil tables (was `fossil rebuild` run on it?); restore it from a backup $ gos v verify --repository ~/demo/copy.gossil this repository has lost its Gossil tables (was `fossil rebuild` run on it?); restore it from a backup Both commands exit with status 78, and gos v open writes no file in ~/demo/other. Run just issue-demo in the source checkout to repeat these checks with the pinned Fossil 2.29. It runs the ignored test of tests/issue_demo.rs.

title: Track issues beside your files
text: This build is the first part of the issue commands, and it has these limits: Four commands run. They are init, task create, task list and task show. Each other issue command exits with status 69. Tasks are private. No command shares a task or syncs it. No command changes a task. There is no edit, undo or delete, and a task has no tags, links, notes, iteration or assignment. A text field cannot hold [. task create refuses a [ in the title, the description or the metadata, because Markdown backlinks are not ported. The text output is provisional. Its bytes can change. Use --json in a script. Run fossil rebuild on a copy only. Gossil refuses a rebuilt repository, as the section above shows.

title: Exact libsql TEXT retrieval
text: Gossil pins a correction of the libsql 0.10.0 Rust wrapper at c02db34ae8a7e91ca7ab8faee18fe41515626940. The published wrapper truncates TEXT at an embedded NUL and can panic on malformed UTF-8. The correction preserves complete valid text and returns existing errors for invalid text and column indices. Issue 36 tracks integration and the bugfix release.

title: Exact libsql TEXT retrieval
text: Owned values are copied immediately from the existing length-aware view. TEXT uses strict UTF-8 decoding. Public get_str accepts only TEXT and returns InvalidColumnType for nontext or malformed text. Invalid indices return InvalidColumnIndex; column names return None for those indices. Generic wrong-type get  conversions retain their upstream behavior. The companion repository preserves the complete published crate and its MIT license at authenticated baseline 243281163e4a39303322385d5f9537736277026e. Its correction changes the local retrieval paths, makes four existing lifetimes explicit and applies normal formatting. Public Row signatures and error variants stay unchanged. The existing statement/current-row lifetime boundary stays in place. Gossil retains the registry libsql-sys 0.10.0 identity and the complete existing libsql-ffi patch. The wrapper correction changes no engine or C ABI. evidence/libsql-wrapper/provenance.json records the exact source identities, archive and patch digests. The original temporary path-patch packet is retained as evidence; it is not a build input.

title: Exact libsql TEXT retrieval
text: Run these checks from the Gossil repository root: just libsql-wrapper-check just libsql-wrapper-test just check The wrapper checks reject revision, feature, registry-sys and provider drift. They run before the normal type check and in CI. Gossil’s installed strict lint and coverage gates remain unchanged. The companion has an explicit upstream-baseline lint contract. It uses fresh profiles for each executed test target and has no coverage exclusions.
