Verify the actual resolved source and provider path when composing Gossil with another package. tests/libsql_row_text.rs exercises the public erased libsql::Row API. It covers NUL positions, Unicode, malformed UTF-8, storage types, invalid indices, recovery after errors and owned values after rows are dropped. SQLite typeof and hex queries check stored bytes before retrieval checks. These controls do not qualify other libsql features or platforms. The retained consuming replays use the same full Git revision. The VCS registration matrix passed all 21 corruption cases with no accepted corruption, provider panic or application or working-file mutation. Four unchanged Gest fidelity tests also passed. Their receipts are under evidence/libsql-wrapper/consuming-replays/. These focused runs do not qualify the complete VCS or Gest feature sets. The wrapper correction was integrated for Gossil 0.4.1 and retained in the released 0.5.0 tracking baseline and later timeline delivery in v0.8.0. The prepared glob module adds a direct exact 0.10.0 FFI edge to the same selected engine. It changes no wrapper pin or provider patch. The 2026-11-21 focused checkpoint retained the complete nonroot graph and passed the focused runtime controls with 0.10.0. Complete frozen-tree qualification is separate; historical glob runs used 0.9.30. The development guide separates current source preparation from recorded releases and installed previews. Writing follows nossaifd guidance, including Rosalind Reid’s communication principles, Shreya Shankar’s plain-writing guidance and Oskar Austegard’s revision method.

title: Exact libsql TEXT retrieval
text: Prefer the full reviewed Git revision over a moving branch. Run the composition checks and public Row controls before changing the pin.

title: Strict local records and metered queries
text: Gossil will keep some of its own records in the local database as JSON, for example the saved ceilings of a file operation. A later reader of such a record must refuse malformed input. It must also stop at fixed limits of work, because a damaged or hostile database can hold a very large or deeply nested record. Three internal modules of src/storage/ give the base for such a reader: command_codec.rs decodes and encodes strict local JSON against one work ledger. operation_limits.rs joins the ceilings of one file operation and their saved form. metered_query.rs charges the size of a query result before it reads the rows. The modules have no public API. The metered content methods below use metered_query.rs. The issue ticket writer calls the put method and metered_query.rs, and no production code calls the other modules yet. The record readers of catalog 6 are the first planned production callers of the other modules. Until they exist, an expect(dead_code) attribute on each module states that no production code calls it. When production code calls every item of a module, the lint fails on the attribute, so that someone removes it. The modules follow these rules from CHANGE-06 of the planned changes of the product specification: Reject wrong types, duplicate JSON keys and unknown fields before any local effect. Charge every limit cumulatively, and do not reset an allowance inside a helper.

title: Strict local records and metered queries
section: Decode a record with one ledger
text: A work ledger is a CodecWork value. It starts from a CodecLimits value with three ceilings: Ceiling What it counts bytes Serialized JSON bytes, for every document that the ledger reads or writes nodes JSON values and object keys; {"a":[1]} counts four depth Nesting of values, with the root at depth one; at most 127 CodecWork::new refuses a zero ceiling and a depth above 127. The ledger keeps one remaining count of each kind for the whole operation. Each call subtracts from it, and no call adds to it. So the second record of an operation can fail on a limit that it alone does not reach. CodecWork::document charges the bytes of a document first. It then decodes the JSON and charges one node for each value and each key. It refuses these inputs: a byte, node or depth limit that the document exceeds a duplicate key in any object, at any depth malformed JSON and input after the first document When the method refuses a document, the ledger keeps the work that the document spent before the refusal. A refusal from the decoder keeps the error of serde_json as its source.

title: Strict local records and metered queries
text: CodecWork::closed_record decodes a closed record. A closed record is a JSON object with exactly the fields that the caller lists. The method first calls document, so it refuses duplicate keys and exhausted limits. Then it refuses these records: a value that is not an object a field that the list does not hold a listed field that the object does not hold, even an optional one The last rule follows CHANGE-06, which requires an explicit null for an optional field. Then the method decodes the object into its Rust type and refuses a field of the wrong type. The method checks only the top-level fields. To close a nested object, give its Rust type the attribute #[serde(deny_unknown_fields)].

title: Strict local records and metered queries
text: CodecWork::encode_record writes the JSON of a record into a buffer that stops at the remaining bytes. It then decodes the output with document, so the output also pays its node and depth work. Output that does not fit is refused, and the refusal spends no work. CodecWork::admit_serialized charges the nodes and the depth of a value without writing any output. A test checks that it charges the same nodes and depth as a strict decode of the output. It refuses the raw JSON encoding of serde_json and a map key that is not a string, a number or a boolean. CodecWork::charge charges bytes for a buffer that the caller allocates itself. remaining_bytes and remaining_nodes report the unused work, so that an owner can charge an outer ledger with the same amounts.

title: Strict local records and metered queries
section: Narrow the ceilings to saved ones
text: A saved record can carry its own ceilings. CodecWork::constrain lowers each ceiling of the ledger to the smaller of the current and the saved value. It keeps every charge made before. A larger saved ceiling does not replenish work. If the saved ceilings are invalid, or lower than the work already spent, the method refuses them and leaves the ledger unchanged. The owner must then abort its operation.

title: Strict local records and metered queries
section: Join the ceilings of a file operation
text: FileOperationLimits::new joins the ceilings of one complete file operation: the native content Limits the artifact parser ParseLimits the FileSystemLimits of paths, plan rows and directory entries the bytes of a saved recipe, the objects of the file closure and the derived rows It refuses a zero ceiling and an output ceiling above i32::MAX. declared gives all eighteen ceilings as a DeclaredBudgets value. That value is the closed saved form, and DeclaredBudgets::FIELDS lists its field names for closed_record. check_saved accepts a saved declaration only when each saved ceiling is valid and at most the ceiling of the current caller. So a saved declaration can narrow a later operation and never widen it. The check grants no authority over a journal or a recipe. codec derives the CodecLimits of the operation from the recipe bytes and the parser ceilings. It caps the depth at 127. root gives the unchanged AdmissionLimits of the content and the parser.

title: Strict local records and metered queries
section: Charge a query before its rows
text: A metered query runs on a WriteTransaction and spends a SqlWork value. That value holds the remaining result rows and payload bytes of the operation. query_bound_sql_work takes fixed internal SQL, its bound parameters and the exact number of result columns, from 1 to 128. It does these steps: Charge one row and 32 bytes for a preflight query. Run the preflight query. It counts the rows of the result and sums the bytes of its text and blob cells. Text counts in UTF-8 bytes, not in characters, so é counts as two bytes. Charge those rows, and 16 bytes for each cell plus the summed bytes. Run the query, and refuse a result whose rows, width or text and blob bytes differ from the charge. The check runs after the rows are read. Each charge subtracts both the rows and the bytes, or neither. query_bound_work also charges the decoded content Budget of the operation, for the bound parameters before the preflight and for the retained cells before the query. Each failure latches in the transaction, as every other storage failure does. Later SQL on that transaction returns the first failure, and rollback returns it too. In a test, the method refuses a query with one row too few of work, and one with one byte too few. The test then reopens the database and finds the rollback complete, and a retry with enough work succeeds. Do not pass caller-supplied SQL to these methods. The preflight wraps the SQL in a common table expression, so only fixed internal SQL is safe.

title: Strict local records and metered queries
text: Four more methods of WriteTransaction spend one SqlWork and one content Budget for a complete content operation: put_private_file_content_budget_with_sql stores private file bytes. read_owner_content_budget_with_sql reads and reconstructs content as the owner. validate_principal_with_sql checks the identity of the repository and the owner, the schema, the policy, the checkout count and the native markers. The two content methods call it before their first content query. validate_catalog_with_sql checks the schema. validate_principal_with_sql calls it. Every query of these methods is a metered query, so each method charges each result row and each retained cell before it reads the rows. The schema check also charges the bytes of the fingerprint encoding of the schema. It builds that encoding before it compares the fingerprint. The issue ticket writer is the one production caller of the metered put. The full proof of catalog 6 accepts a private row only for a check-in, a file of a check-in or an issue artifact. So a put that no issue owns leaves a repository that gos v verify refuses. The unit tests of the put use it only on fixture files. A put charges its input to the content Budget as decoded bytes. A put that writes also charges the compressed envelope as stored bytes. It charges the envelope again as decoded bytes, because the write keeps the bound value until the write ends. The methods keep these rules of the unmetered methods of the content boundary in content.rs: A put verifies the full native name of the bytes before any SQL. Bytes that a public receipt names stay public, and a put adds no private row for them. A put does not store identical bytes again. It reads the stored bytes back and verifies them against their name, which the new bytes already match. A phantom is an artifact whose bytes are missing. Full bytes replace a phantom, and they replace a delta whose baseline is missing. The put removes the old delta row and the phantom row. An orphan, a delta or a required typed record that waits on the phantom stops that replacement. A read verifies the size and the full name of each link of a delta chain. In a read, a missing, phantom or shunned baseline makes the content unavailable. The constant NEWEST_CATALOG in schema.rs names the newest catalog, which is catalog 6 in this build. The metered methods admit only that catalog. They refuse a repository at catalog 1 with the message repository catalog 1 is not the newest catalog 6. The older unmetered methods still admit catalog 1. Each failure of these methods latches in the transaction, so an earlier write in the same transaction does not survive the rollback. The issue ticket writer calls the put method and the read method.

title: Strict local records and metered queries
text: The tests live in tests/support/storage_command_codec.rs, tests/support/storage_operation_limits.rs, tests/support/storage_metered_query.rs and tests/support/storage_content_metered.rs. They run as unit tests of the storage module. The metered query and metered content tests use a real libSQL file, and the content fixtures come from the product initializer at catalog 6. The content tests follow the cases CONTENT-01 to CONTENT-08 of the content boundary contract of the specification. All the tests check each limit at the last value that it accepts and at the next value, which it refuses.

title: Strict local records and metered queries
text: The code comes from uncommitted work in the worktree gest-native-core-integration. These parts of that work were left out: strict decoding with a one-time ledger, and the charges for scope arrays and scope names the unmetered query routes and the query that reads its column count the restore of saved limits that only the tests used the content put that takes a caller budget without SQL work, which is an unmetered route the budget accessors that only the tests used, and the getter of the remaining work, with no caller the admission of catalogs 2, 5 and 6, and the routes that only old catalogs need all of retained_file.rs, which needs the excluded modules native_checkout, checkout_fs and file_command, and whose history proof is used only for migration The port also follows these rules from the independent review of that work: test only behavior keep metered_query internal run rustfmt on every line do not call unwrap on stored data

title: Strict local records and metered queries
text: Give each operation one CodecWork, one SqlWork and one content Budget, and pass them to every record and query of the operation. Decode each saved record with closed_record.

title: Local database ownership
text: API: LocalStore gives the exact contract. The storage module opens local libSQL files and owns one write transaction at a time. Its low-level lifecycle API also supports the validated native storage boundary. That boundary installs the complete schema and implements empty-root initialization, one native directory registration, explicit tracking and scopes, private file recording and bounded catalog1 content operations. The native storage guide defines the catalog formats. Opening that higher-level repository validates its stored root and authority metadata. Migration and broader adapters remain unimplemented. Both LocalOwnerRepository::create and LocalOwnerRepository::initialize refuse existing -journal, -wal and -shm entries beside the destination before creating the database. They preserve those entries, including dangling symlinks and directories. Observation failures retain the operating-system cause. The checks append literal native filename suffixes. They observe the namespace before creation and again before SQLite entry. Callers must keep that namespace stable through engine cleanup. The constructors observe regular-file identity at separate boundaries. These observations do not establish atomic binding to an engine handle. Checkout-free initialization retains a failed main file if the engine might have opened it or COMMIT was attempted. It reports cleanup uncertainty separately from the first operation error.

title: Local database ownership
text: use gossil::storage::{LocalStore, StorageError}; async fn lifecycle(path: &std::path::Path) -> Result  { let mut store = LocalStore::open(path).await?; store.begin_write().await?.commit().await?; store.begin_write().await?.rollback().await?; Ok(()) } The example opens the database and terminates empty transactions. Use LocalOwnerRepository for admitted native content operations. The example above uses only the low-level lifecycle API. LocalStore::open(path) builds a local database and retains one connection. It treats nonempty paths as literal native filenames, including relative names that begin with file: and names that contain ?, # or %. On Unix, it preserves filename bytes that are not valid UTF-8 when the filesystem accepts them. A filesystem rejection remains an open error. An embedded NUL returns an error with the original std::ffi::NulError cause. An empty path retains SQLite’s temporary-database behavior and fails the required WAL check. Every file open sets and reads back WAL, foreign keys ON, synchronous=FULL and a 5000 ms busy timeout. WAL is SQLite’s write-ahead journal mode. An open fails if configuration differs from these requirements. begin_write(&mut self) takes the connection before it issues BEGIN IMMEDIATE. The returned WriteTransaction, the transaction owner, exclusively borrows the store. A second owner cannot borrow it at the same time. There is no public SQL, connection, statement or lazy query interface. An internal execution error marks the owner rollback-only, which means later internal operations cannot issue SQL and commit must reject the operation. Queries materialize results by collecting rows into owned values before returning. They consume their statements and rows inside the owner. Preparation, stepping and value-decoding errors follow the same failure path. The native content operations also latch non-SQL failures through the owner. Fixture SQL uses the same private execution and row-collection code as the storage boundary. Explicit commit and rollback return the connection only after SQLite reports that no transaction remains active. A commit error triggers checked rollback when the transaction remains active. Errors retain the original engine cause and report a separate cleanup failure when one occurs. If commit fails but checked rollback restores an idle connection, the store can begin another write. The commit still returns its original error. commit_checked() returns a CommitFailure with the original operation error and an optional cleanup error. Both retain their typed source chains through StorageError::source() when an underlying cause exists. Inspect operation first and cleanup separately. commit() keeps its existing StorageError result and stores cleanup diagnostics as text. A failed BEGIN or cleanup discards the connection and poisons the store. A poisoned store requires an explicit new open.

title: Local database ownership
text: Dropping a WriteTransaction without explicit termination poisons the store and drops its sole connection. The destructor executes no SQL and polls no future. The pinned local libSQL connection uses SQLite’s close_v2 API. SQLite rolls back an active transaction when the connection is destroyed. This depends on the module keeping statements and other connection aliases inside the owner. Local SQL calls block their current asynchronous poll, including busy waits. The cancellation fixture aborts at a controlled await between SQL calls and awaits task destruction before checking writer progress. Cancellation after a successful COMMIT leaves committed rows in the database. It cannot undo a commit whose result the outer caller has not received. A later server adapter must define its blocking scheduling and result-delivery boundaries.

title: Local database ownership
text: LocalStore supplies transaction ownership. LocalOwnerRepository adds the repository, checkout and history checks required by the private recording library. Opening a LocalStore alone does not establish those prerequisites. The recorder validates the complete supported history, captures every explicitly private tracked file, and writes content, a manifest, its receipt and derived rows in one transaction. Helpers borrow the operation’s content budget and parser ledger throughout. Failure rolls back earlier database writes, and recording never writes the working files. The qualification record distinguishes the checked library checkpoint from the CLI awaiting final gates. It does not add public SQL access or change the lifecycle guarantees above.

title: Local database ownership
text: Use LocalStore to own a transaction, or LocalOwnerRepository for validated repository operations. Prefer commit_checked() when a caller needs to inspect both error causes. Next, consult the generated Rust API for the chosen type’s signatures and errors.

title: Native local storage
text: API: LocalOwnerRepository gives the exact contract. The storage API creates an empty native repository without a checkout. After registration, its catalog6 library can track paths, select explicit scopes and record the complete private tracked tree through one owned libSQL transaction. The shared history remains the initial empty check-in. General artifact crosslinks, Gest projections and filesystem recovery remain planned. Catalog names identify storage formats. Catalog1 binds a checkout at creation and supports bounded private content bytes. Catalog6 starts without a checkout and supports one later registration. Generic catalog1 content writes remain separate from catalog6 recording.

title: Native local storage
text: LocalOwnerRepository::initialize(path, InitializeOptions) creates a native repository without registering a checkout. Supply the project and local owner identities, administrator, password, SQLite date expression, SHA1 selection and finite content/parser limits. The API requires an explicit administrator. It does not read environment variables or a preference database. The vcs init CLI adapter supplies generated identities and a password, and chooses the administrator from options or the environment. It uses this strict catalog6 contract; it does not bind a checkout. Initialization normalizes the date for the root D card. It installs the native default report, system users and administrator password digest. SHA1 selection sets the native hash policy and hashes the actual root with SHA1. Otherwise the root uses SHA3-256. initialization_identity() returns the stored project-code and server-code after checking admission. This constructor installs catalog6 with checkout_count=0. Its only nonempty g_* tables are g_storage, g_local_owner and g_public_receipt. Check a repository says what open, each command and gos v verify check in a catalog6 repository. The full proof of gos v verify authenticates the single canonical empty root, its native hash, date, event, branch tags and receive/index facts. The remaining local tables must be empty, except for the exact registration, tracking, scope and private recording inventories described below. The full proof refuses extra native content or indexed history outside that family. It accepts private issue tickets written before, between or after check-ins. It checks each row of a ticket against the artifact of that ticket, as the issue ticket guide says. The tables g_project_binding and g_checkout_project are empty, or each holds the one binding row that issue init writes. The row binds the registered checkout to a project. No upgrade occurs on open. Open refuses a repository before any effect when its catalog marker, the storage_version value of g_storage, names catalog2, catalog4 or catalog5. The message names the catalog found and catalog6, and the CLI exits 78. Gossil has no upgrade path before its first real release, so the fix is a new repository. Open reads the marker before it switches the file to WAL, the write-ahead log mode of SQLite. So a refused file keeps every byte. Open refuses an unknown marker, such as 3 or 7, and a missing marker with exit 1. Generic private content writes through this handle refuse catalog6. The destination and its recovery neighbors must remain stable through engine cleanup. Existing destinations and recovery entries are preserved. Failures retain the first cause and report cleanup uncertainty separately. A possibly opened engine or an attempted commit prevents automatic main-file removal. Pathname observations do not certify engine disposal or atomic binding. Templates, global preferences and project display fields are outside this API.

title: Native local storage
text: After checkout-free initialization, call LocalOwnerRepository::register_checkout(checkout_id, root, limits) to register one existing directory against the initial empty root. This API supports only catalog6 with no existing registration. It refuses catalog1 and a second registration, including a retry with the same ID or an alias of the same root. Supply a nonempty, NUL-free checkout ID of at most 1024 UTF-8 bytes. Supply an existing directory with a nonempty, NUL-free UTF-8 path of at most 4096 bytes, both before and after canonicalization. Both ceilings also use the smaller limits.parser.input_bytes. Relative paths and caller aliases resolve to the canonical directory. Persisted roots must retain their exact canonical spelling, device, inode and owner binding on every admission. Canonical components are observed without following links. Callers must keep the namespace stable. These pathname observations do not protect against hostile concurrent replacement. Registration uses one exclusive database transaction. It runs the checks of each command, and checks that no checkout row exists, before writing one checkout row, one owner row and checkout_count=1. It writes exactly the three native keys checkout, checkout-hash and fingerprint. These keys retain the actual initial root RID, its hash and the native fingerprint derived from the receive record. The API runs the checks of each command again on the result before checked commit. Earlier writes roll back on failure. The lifecycle rules still govern commit and cleanup uncertainty. The returned CheckoutView owns the repository ID, checkout ID, canonical root, shared head, combined head, generation and pending version. The combined head selects the owner’s private tree together with the shared tree, which is empty in this recording family. At registration, the shared head is the public initial root, the combined head is absent, and both counters are zero. A later private recording advances the combined head while the shared head stays fixed. checkout_view(checkout_id, limits) authenticates that exact persisted registration. checkout_view_for_root(root, limits) authenticates the sole registration for the explicitly chosen canonical root. Both methods run the checks of each command and refuse a changed owner, invalid bindings or unsupported inventory. Root lookup refuses absence, another root, unauthorized ownership and multiple registrations. It allocates no identity and repairs no registration or native key. Ordinary files and nested Git repositories in the directory remain unselected and unchanged. Registration creates no file check-in, materializes no files and publishes no ROOT/.gossil/checkout.json locator. These methods require no Gest project, issue or author initialization. The source vcs open adapter composes these library methods with locator publication and recovery. Its explicit flags still use the same admission and publisher rules. Root lookup itself only gives authenticated facts and does not recover a locator. Reopen accepts exactly zero or one such catalog6 registration. It checks the checkout and owner rows against checkout_count, and the three native keys against the head of the checkout. The full proof of gos v verify checks the supported recording history. Generic private content writes still refuse catalog6.

title: Native local storage
text: This source checkout exposes LocalOwnerRepository::add_files and LocalOwnerRepository::pending_adds, with TrackingLimits and PendingAdd. Call add_files(checkout, paths, wanted, limits, tracking) with the exact CheckoutView from this owner as wanted, plus finite admission and tracking limits. The wanted view states the complete checkout state that the caller expects before mutation. The method validates the whole batch and cumulative inventory, reads and rechecks each regular file, then returns the committed view. The method rejects the batch if the heads, generation or pending version are stale, or if the owner changed. It also checks that each table that must stay empty, such as the pending removes, is empty. Use the returned view for the next mutation. pending_adds(checkout, limits, tracking) returns the complete bounded pending inventory in pathname order. tracked_paths lists both pending and recorded paths, and path_scopes reads only explicit scope choices. PendingAdd::executable records the mode at first enrollment. Later mode changes do not alter that flag until recording captures the current file. Only this producer’s exact catalog6 state is admitted. New g_vfile rows use the current combined-head vid, or the initial root before recording. They use rid=mrid=0, regular-file link flags, executable mode and observed modification time. A RID is a native artifact row identifier. New batches retain earlier rows and advance pending_version once. Existing-only batches recheck files but change no state. g_pending_path remains empty. New paths have no g_path_scope row, and add preserves earlier explicit choices. Catalog1 rules remain unchanged. No file bytes, canonical artifacts, receipts or file-containing check-ins are stored by add. Working bytes remain unchanged. TrackingLimits bounds the complete inventory and batch count, bytes per path, path components, initial captured working bytes and read buffer size. The final recheck temporarily retains another copy of one captured file. The captured-byte limit therefore does not bound total process memory. The methods reject zero structural or buffer bounds. Capture, recapture and comparison also charge the operation’s borrowed content budget, including retained parent-directory checks. The cumulative work bounds do not measure all process allocations. Captured bytes exist only for transaction validation. Paths and descriptor identities must satisfy the CLI path contract. The protected database identities come from the store’s retained private FileIdentity; callers cannot supply replacement authority. New additions have unselected scope. An absent scope row means neither shared nor private. Add alone authorizes no recording or sync.

title: Native local storage
text: Call initialize, register_checkout, add_files, select_path_scopes, then commit_private_tracked_files. Registration, add, scope selection and changed recording return checkout views. Pass the most recent returned view as the expected view and set request.scope to PathScope::Private. The storage API gives the exact signatures. Supply finite AdmissionLimits for content and parsing, plus TrackingLimits for path counts, path sizes and retained working bytes. Private recording saves the current bytes and executable modes of every tracked file as one complete private history snapshot. Scope is each path’s explicit shared or private choice. Private means owner-local history; shared marks a path for shared history, whose recording and synchronization are not supported here. Every tracked path must have private scope before this recorder can run. The library checkpoint has passed its recorded checks; the CLI checkpoint still needs final qualification. The examples describe source contracts and establish no release or installation. See development status for the accepted tracking baseline and remaining work. select_path_scopes(checkout, wanted, selections, limits, tracking) persists immutable explicit choices for tracked paths. An equal batch is a checked no-op; a conflicting choice rejects the whole batch. A batch with new choices advances pending_version once. Like add, scope selection checks that each table that must stay empty is empty. path_scopes reads only explicit choices; tracked_paths returns the complete ordered tracked inventory. Neither read infers missing scopes. commit_private_tracked_files(checkout, request, limits, tracking) requires PathScope::Private and a nonempty, duplicate-free set of all tracked paths. It rejects an empty path set, including when the checkout has no tracked paths. Each path must have a persisted private choice. request.expected supplies all seven CheckoutView fields. They are repository ID, checkout ID, registered root, shared head, combined head, generation and pending version. Stale expectations or failed owner validation cause the transaction to reject the request. Catalog1 stores loose private content bytes without a file tree. Catalog6 recording stores a complete file tree and its admitted history. The request supplies actor, comment and native date bytes. The actor is nonempty UTF-8 without NUL. The comment is UTF-8 with no NUL or literal left bracket. Fossil’s comment format uses left brackets to start links. Excluding them keeps the backlink table outside this bounded family. No alternative escape for a literal left bracket is supported. The date must use the native date grammar and be strictly later than every parent, including under native SQL date conversion. The recorder captures all working files again, retaining their bytes and executable modes within finite limits. Edits after add are included without a second add. Capture and parser helpers borrow one content budget and one parser work ledger, which count cumulative work across the whole operation. A request explicitly supplies all tracked paths and the current view: use gossil::storage::{CheckoutView, PathScope, PrivateRecordingRequest}; fn request ( view: &'a CheckoutView, paths: &'a [&'a str], // Every tracked path, not a selected subset. ) -> PrivateRecordingRequest  { PrivateRecordingRequest { expected: view, paths, scope: PathScope::Private, actor: b"Owner", comment: b"Save notes", date: b"2026-11-20T12:00:01", } } Select private scope first. Use a date later than the root and previous private recording. Pass the request to commit_private_tracked_files with explicit limits. Call the initial shared empty root S and private recordings L1, L2 and so on. For example, recording edited notes creates L2 while S stays the shared view. The shared empty root S remains immutable. The first private manifest L1 has parent S; later manifests have parents Lprev then S. Every private manifest contains the complete tree. Keeping S as a parent preserves the explicit shared base while the first parent follows private history. A commit reads only its parent and the parent of that parent, so its cost does not grow with the history. It checks every field of the tracked rows and the tables that must stay empty. It checks its parent in full against the grandparent, which means the canonical bytes, comment, receipt, date, unchanged files and the absence of deletions. So a commit never stores a check-in that the full proof then refuses. Later additions use the current combined-head RID as their vid. A projection is a derived database row. The full proof of gos v verify validates the whole history and the exact native and local projections, including private content, parent, event, leaf, file-link and checkout facts. It rejects a file link whose content hash differs from the hash in its manifest. Catalog6 recording accepts full compressed content and refuses physical deltas. Catalog1 retains its separate delta reconstruction contract. Content that already exists is verified and reused without rewriting its receipt or privacy class. General removal and rename remain unsupported. Recorded.native_name is the new manifest/check-in hash. Recorded also returns the refreshed view after checked commit. NoChange validates metadata, dates, bytes and modes but creates no receipt and changes no head or counter. Changed recording writes one local receipt, payloads, manifest and projections atomically. It advances both generation and pending version once. Working files remain unchanged. Shared recording and synchronization remain unsupported. Catalog1 content operations keep their separate contract. The source CLI exposes scope selection and private recording and inspects recorded states through status. A failed write of the CLI receipt to standard output leaves the recorded history durable.

title: Native local storage
text: LocalOwnerRepository::create installs catalog1, exclusively creates the database file and binds its repository, owner and checkout identities. The initial root contains native C, D, R, T, U and Z records. The parser validates those bytes with date conversion on the same owned SQL connection. Creation installs all six accepted schema files, native markers, compressed root content, native crosslinks, owner, checkout and public receipt together. The final complete-policy marker follows those writes. A failed creation rolls back the schema writes. Root construction computes the encoded user length and complete canonical length before allocating either output. The size calculation and encoder use the same existing token escape rules. Private decoding boundaries check fully stepped native date values and owned catalog fields. A failure rolls back earlier writes in the transaction. Metadata errors preserve the underlying operating-system cause. LocalOwnerRepository::open requires an existing readable and writable regular file. Its explicit AdmissionLimits bound root reconstruction and parsing. For the bound catalog1 constructor, admission checks canonical bytes, native branch tags and event, the public receipt, checkout bindings, complete policy and native versions. The receipt must identify the root itself with validation class local-explicit-publication. The event fields and both branch tags must match the canonical root, including absent event overrides. Admission rejects native or valid typed projections that claim the empty root produces another artifact type or requires a graph dependency. It also rejects current file, merge, path-selection and journal rows outside the empty checkout. A producer identifies the artifact that creates a fact. A target identifies what a fact refers to. Admission distinguishes those roles rather than rejecting every row that mentions the root. In catalog1, operational and provenance rows, invalid diagnostic records and historical selection records can remain. Unrelated private blobs and physical deltas can remain, including a private delta whose baseline is the public root. These rows do not extend the supported public graph or implement their corresponding product operations. AdmissionLimits bound content reconstruction and parser work. Catalog1 admission validates its root. Catalog6 open checks only the facts whose cost does not grow with the history, and charges retained metadata to the same operation budget. Fixed scalar conflict queries bound the data they return. Neither mechanism sets a ceiling on SQLite scan work across stored tables. Operating-system access establishes the local owner boundary. A stored owner ID is a binding, and callers cannot turn an ID string into permission. shared_view() returns a restricted local view with no owner operations. Network authentication and team principals remain unimplemented. The shared view reads the initial public root only. An absent name and a private file name return the same unavailable error. A private association with already public root bytes preserves their public classification. A receipt for an unsupported general graph cannot grant shared access.

title: Native local storage
text: Gossil checks a catalog6 repository in three places, which are open, each command and gos v verify. Open checks only the facts whose cost does not grow with the history. SQLite and its foreign keys must be on. Open checks the catalog marker, the fingerprint, the project-code and server-code config rows, the schema and the policy. It checks checkout_count and the one registration, with its pending_version bounded by the generation and the tracked rows. It checks the project binding, whose IDs must all be text. Open replays no artifact, compares no table, checks no hash and runs no foreign key scan. Each command checks what it reads and writes, in its own transaction. A write never stores an artifact that verify then refuses because of a fact that the write read. A read checks what it prints against what it parses. The issue ticket guide, private recording and recorded ancestry give the checks of each command. gos v verify gives the full proof. It replays every check-in and every issue artifact and compares each table with that replay. Only a scan of the history or of a whole table can check some facts. Commands trust these facts, and only verify checks them. This guide calls them the trusted class. Examples are rows that no index of a command reaches, link rows, the amended user and comment columns euser and ecomment of event, and foreign key integrity. An edit by the owner that keeps every fact consistent with every other fact was never detectable by open, by a command or by verify. A stock fossil rebuild drops every table that Fossil does not know, so it drops each g_ table. Open then refuses the repository, and the CLI exits 78 with this message: this repository has lost its Gossil tables (was `fossil rebuild` run on it?); restore it from a backup A stock fossil push or fossil sync sends no private artifact and empties unsent. A push, sync or pull adds the config rows last-sync-url and hash-policy. The push is safe. verify admits an unsent table that holds any subset of the rows that replay gives, and every command still works after the push. But verify still refuses an unsent row that replay does not give. A push leaves unclustered unchanged, and so does a sync or pull that receives nothing. So verify still requires that unclustered hold exactly the rows that replay gives. A pull or sync that receives a public artifact adds rows to blob, unclustered and other tables, and verify refuses the repository. By default, a commit in a checkout of a clone has the same effect, because autosync pushes the commit back into the Gossil file. Gossil does not support receiving artifacts yet. A command keeps no snapshot of the repository between transactions. So an owner sees each commit that another process makes after the open, and needs no second open. The CLI retries a command once only after database is locked. Catalog1 keeps its snapshot, because its operations do not check what they read. A sealed admission proof records SQLite data_version, connection total_changes and exact durable authority metadata. Each catalog1 content operation checks that proof under its writer reservation before a private lookup. The saved metadata includes the root-conflict predicates. Refreshing only the connection counter cannot accept a newly contradictory projection. An unrelated external commit conservatively requires explicit readmission. Unexpected writes on the same connection also require readmission. In catalog1, supported private file operations refresh only total_changes after checked commit or rollback. They preserve the admitted root and policy, and they never advance the saved data_version. Future root or policy mutation APIs must invalidate or replace the proof after full validation. Content operations do not decode the root through a hidden admission budget. They check durable authority and charge requested content to caller limits. Creation and open use their separate, explicit admission limits.

title: Native local storage
text: For a bound catalog1 repository, use put_private_file_content to store private bytes. Use read_content to retrieve content through LocalOwnerRepository. Every content read or write receives finite Limits. Those limits bound each stored envelope, decoded output, chain depth and aggregate stored and decoded work. Reconstruction checks every intermediate native size and full hash. A RID is a native artifact row identifier. A visited-RID set rejects cycles. A phantom is an artifact whose content is missing. Shunned artifacts are excluded by repository policy. Missing, phantom and shunned baselines reject successful reconstruction. The four-byte big-endian envelope retains native codec behavior. Excess capacity and bytes after the first complete zlib stream are accepted. Exact repository size and hash still have to match. A short NoPayload result cannot stand in for valid empty content. compression::pack_bounded uses the existing encoder and checks the full stored length before each output reservation. Its ceiling includes the header. The encoder also uses a fixed 8192-byte working buffer and backend state. The ceiling is not a bound on every allocation in the process. A hash, policy, codec, schema or resource error makes the borrowed owner rollback-only. Catching the error cannot permit later SQL or successful commit. Earlier writes in that transaction also roll back. Full bytes can replace a phantom or a delta target whose old baseline is missing. Replacement removes the stale delta row and clears phantom state. Typed dependents are records in the adapter projections that require the content. Required orphan, delta or typed dependents cause an explicit refusal until their native and typed crosslinks are implemented.

title: Native local storage
text: LocalOwnerRepository::recorded_timeline(checkout, limits) returns a complete Vec  for an explicit existing catalog6 checkout. Each row has hash: String, date: Vec , actor: Vec , comment: Vec  and private: bool. The generated Rust API gives the exact signature. Results start with the current private check-in and follow its ancestors to the immutable shared empty root S. The root occurs exactly once, last, with private == false; every private row has private == true. Before any private recording, S is the sole row. The reader follows ancestry rather than sorting rows by date. Accepted recordings have strictly increasing dates. A commit checks the date of its parent, and the full proof refuses equal or backward dates anywhere in the history. Hashes are full verified native identities. Dates preserve native D-card bytes; actor and comment preserve the decoded native U-card and C-card bytes exactly. The supported metadata is UTF-8 without NUL, but these public fields remain byte vectors. The reader does not normalize dates, abbreviate hashes or use edited display metadata. The reader walks every manifest of the chain and reads the event row of each check-in. It refuses an event whose user or comment is not the U or C card of its manifest, and a chain whose length differs from the generation. It reads no file content. The full proof of gos v verify checks the rest of each event row. One transaction runs the checks of each command, walks the manifests and reads their event rows, under one content budget and one parser ledger. The complete result capacity is charged before allocation. The ledger covers the whole chain, so the parser limits bound the length of the history that the timeline can read. Under the CLI limits that is about 500 check-ins of one file. Success returns the entire ancestry only after checked transaction completion. There is no truncation or successful empty history. Missing checkout, changed authority, unsupported or corrupt state, invalid or exhausted limits, allocation, provider and transaction failures return StorageError. The first operation cause and separate cleanup failure retain their existing precedence. This operation reads no working-file contents, makes no durable mutation and publishes no locator. Pending additions and dirty or deleted working files do not change its recorded result. The source timeline and log commands expose this reader as complete compact NDJSON. Existing-locator opening admission is separate from the API operation. Serialization has a third finite allowance derived from the unchanged CLI decoded-content limit. No whole-invocation aggregate budget is claimed. Revision selection, filters and broader Fossil timeline behavior remain deferred.

title: Native local storage
text: Each catalog installs six SQL inputs under src/storage/schema/. Catalog6 substitutes adapter-catalog6.sql for the catalog1 adapter. That file adds the local audit tables transactions, transaction_events and g_command_audit, which stay empty in this build. Initialization also stores the SQL of the installed ticket tables in the native ticket-table setting. A stock fossil rebuild recreates the ticket tables from that setting, so they keep their Gest columns. just catalog-interop checks a new repository with the pinned Fossil reference. It runs fossil test-integrity, then fossil rebuild on a copy, and compares the ticket columns. It then checks a repository with private check-ins and an issue between them, with fossil test-integrity, fossil timeline and fossil ticket show. Last, it makes a stock Fossil repository and checks that verify and open refuse it with exit 78 and change no byte of it. When the reference is absent, it exits 5, the status for not-run. The issue ticket writer stores one private task or project ticket in a catalog 6 repository. open admits a repository that holds such tickets beside private check-ins, and the project binding that issue init writes. LocalOwnerRepository::verify runs the full proof on demand, and verify_issue proves one issue from its own rows. Both read in a transaction that they roll back, so they change nothing. Each proof bounds each artifact and each row. No proof sets a bound on the whole repository. The timeline is the one command that does, because it parses its whole chain under one ledger. The command gos v verify runs both proofs. The required object inventory and complete stored definitions are checked before mutation. Known optional schema families return an unsupported configuration error. Unregistered persistent triggers receive a separate error. Dynamic ticket templates, extension schemas and their registry transitions remain unimplemented. General public receipts, publication, native and typed rebuild, retained-dependency administration and filesystem journals also remain unimplemented. The public APIs do not offer those operations. The internal modules for strict local records are the base for the record readers of catalog 6, which are not built yet.

title: Native local storage
text: Prefer initialize, then register_checkout when one native empty-root registration is needed. Use create for catalog1 private content operations. For private recording, select scopes explicitly and pass the latest complete view and every tracked path to the library recorder. Set finite admission limits, then consult the generated API for repository creation, admission and content methods.

title: Emit a task creation artifact
text: The task_ticket module turns a validated TaskValues snapshot into complete, uncompressed bytes in Fossil’s ticket artifact format. A ticket records work to track, and its artifact is a sequence of newline-terminated records called cards. Gossil uses those cards to carry task fields. Here, native means the Fossil artifact format. The task emitter shares its card syntax, size plan and checksum with the artifact and project emitters, which the Gest ticket guide describes. Use the library to inspect or test task creation artifacts in memory. The issue ticket writer stores a task creation privately in a native repository. The command gos i task create emits a task creation with this module and stores it with that writer. The commands gos i task list and gos i task show read the tasks back. The other issue commands remain separate work.

title: Emit a task creation artifact
text: Validate all eleven decoded fields with task_from_values first. The task values guide shows that step. Given the resulting task, emit an artifact with an explicit byte limit: use gossil::native_date::NativeDate; use gossil::task_ticket::task_creation_bytes; let date = NativeDate::parse(b"2026-11-18T12:00:00.000000001Z").unwrap(); let ticket_id = b"0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567"; let bytes = task_creation_bytes(&task, ticket_id, b"native actor", date, 65_536).unwrap(); assert!(bytes.len() <= 65_536); Use the application setup when calling Gossil from another crate. Handle DateError and TicketError in applications rather than unwrapping the results. A J card assigns a named field to its encoded value. The D card records the artifact creation date, and the U card records its actor. The K card contains the native ticket identity, which requires exactly forty lowercase ASCII hexadecimal bytes. Supply it independently of the task’s gest_id. Gest is a task and artifact tracker. A Gest ID has 32 lowercase letters from k through z and remains a J field. The emitter neither generates identities nor derives one identity from the other. The U card contains caller-supplied actor bytes escaped with the Fossil token codec. These bytes need not be a Gest author ID or UTF-8 text.

title: Emit a task creation artifact
text: NativeDate represents a Gregorian UTC instant as signed i128 nanoseconds since the Unix epoch. Supported years are 0001 through 9999, inclusive. parse accepts YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS[.fraction][Z], where a fraction has one through nine digits. A missing suffix also means UTC. It rejects offsets, leap seconds, year zero, invalid calendars and excess fractional digits. It does not normalize other spellings into this grammar. from_epoch_nanos checks the same year range. epoch_nanos returns the integer value without floating-point conversion. Display and the emitted D card use exactly nine fractional digits and no suffix. This domain is separate from the more permissive Gest business timestamps in TaskValues. The caller supplies the D card date independently of those timestamps.

title: Emit a task creation artifact
text: The artifact has a D card, fourteen J cards sorted by field name, a K card, a U card and a final Z checksum card. Each card ends with a newline. The eleven model fields are assigned_to, created_at, description, gest_id, metadata, priority, project_id, resolved_at, status, title and updated_at. Each uses compact serde_json encoding of the values returned by task_to_values, followed by native token escaping. Strings retain JSON quotes, priority is an integer or null, and metadata retains its JSON value. Status and business timestamps use the normalized forms in the task values contract. Null values remain present. The three fixed fields classify this Gossil record. gossil_deleted is JSON false, marking the creation as not deleted. gossil_kind is raw task, identifying a task record, and gossil_schema is raw 1, identifying its schema version. These fields define Gossil’s task schema; this emitter does not implement a consumer for that schema. The last two values are literal bytes rather than JSON strings. This function emits complete creation snapshots. It emits neither field-appending updates that extend existing field values nor cards that link a parent artifact to record ancestry. See the artifact parser guide for supported structural card forms. The Z card holds the lowercase MD5 checksum of all preceding artifact bytes. max_output bounds the complete encoded artifact, including token expansion, card syntax, checksum and newlines. The effective limit also respects isize::MAX. An exact-size limit succeeds; a smaller limit returns TicketError::Size. The limit is an output bound, rather than a total heap budget. The emitter counts borrowed model values before retaining serialized JSON or reserving the output buffer. Bookkeeping allocations have fixed bounds independent of task string and metadata sizes. The identifier, status and timestamp strings, the fourteen-field list and the checksum still allocate. Even a zero output limit can therefore allocate fixed bookkeeping; the limit does not cap all memory use. TicketError::TicketId rejects malformed K bytes. Allocation retains a fallible reservation error, Token retains a token codec error, and Json retains a serialization error. The generated API documents these variants. The gest_ticket module defines TicketError, and task_ticket re-exports it. Its Size message is ticket output limit, because the task, artifact and project emitters all return it.

title: Emit a task creation artifact
text: Check raw field presence, duplicate keys and input byte limits before constructing TaskValues. Choose the native ticket identity, actor, D instant and output budget independently of the task’s model fields. The emitter performs no clock reads, identity generation or database writes. It does not replay history, check references to other records or determine who may write a task. A future repository operation must define and enforce those rules, including any requirement that artifact dates increase. Emission alone does not establish Fossil engine compatibility. Repository migration must separately validate and store any existing records. This page follows the nossaifd writing guide, including principles credited to Rosalind Reid, Shreya Shankar and Oskar Austegard.

title: Emit a task creation artifact
text: Use task_from_values to validate a snapshot, then call task_creation_bytes with an explicit output limit. Next, inspect the returned bytes or use them in application tests, and handle emission errors. Repository storage integration remains planned.

title: Fossil token bytes
text: API: fossilize gives the exact contract. The gossil::token_codec module encodes and decodes arbitrary bytes for Fossil artifact and protocol tokens. It implements the token escape functions from Fossil revision b3a1c8efb2731dffbd5cc38c58ac349746de6da6, src/encode.c:392-458. It does not parse artifacts or select repository hash policy.

title: Fossil token bytes
text: All three functions return Result and preserve allocation error causes. fossilize encodes the entire slice, including embedded NUL bytes. fossilize_c_string encodes bytes before the first NUL, or the whole slice when no NUL occurs. Both return bytes without a C terminator. The eight escaped bytes are NUL, space, tab, newline, carriage return, vertical tab, form feed and backslash. Their escape letters are 0, s, t, n, r, v, f and backslash. Each follows a backslash. Other bytes pass through unchanged. No function requires UTF-8. defossilize stops reading at the first source NUL or the slice end. Unknown escapes discard the backslash. For example, \q decodes to q. A terminal backslash survives. The returned DecodedToken.bytes contains every emitted byte, including bytes emitted after a decoded NUL. Its c_string_len is the first decoded NUL index, or the output length. C-string consumers see only that prefix. use gossil::token_codec::{defossilize, fossilize}; let encoded = fossilize(b"a b\0").unwrap(); let decoded = defossilize(&encoded).unwrap(); assert_eq!(decoded.bytes, b"a b\0"); assert_eq!(decoded.c_string_len, 3); The implementation checks the exact encoded size and reserves output storage before emitting bytes. TokenError::Size rejects arithmetic overflow or lengths above Rust vector capacity. TokenError::Allocation retains the allocator error. These errors are Rust resource policies. The C comparison requires valid pointers, terminated C strings and explicit lengths within allocated storage. It excludes signed C integer overflow and allocation exhaustion.

title: Fossil token bytes
text: Use the contracts above with explicit resource limits. Next, consult the generated Rust API for the full signatures and errors.

title: Working with repositories
text: Use this guide to plan which agent files to track, how to review changes, and how to connect tasks to exact file versions. Plan the history around a task, its plan and the evidence behind a decision. Git remains the source-code authority. Gossil is designed to give the surrounding agent work its own history and sharing rules. Most of this page describes planned repository workflows. The source CLI supports empty repository initialization and three file-delta diagnostics. Initialization creates no checkout and selects no files. The source vcs open command registers one checkout at the empty root, or reopens it with supported private history and locator recovery. The source also supports explicit tracking, scope selection and private recording. Its Rust library implements the corresponding storage contracts. Library registration selects no files and publishes no locator, the local file that lets commands find and verify a checkout. Catalog1 private content operations follow their separate native storage contract. The private recording library saves the complete tracked tree within the resource limits in its storage contract. It does not provide shared recording or issue management. The Fossil references teach the inherited workflow; their commands are not Gossil aliases.

title: Working with repositories
text:
A separately installed development preview supports a small local file workflow. This unmerged preview is not a release, and full qualification is incomplete. Use a disposable folder and copies of files, and keep Git as the source authority. These commands require that preview’s installed gos or gossil executable. The source CLI supports init, native open, add, status, scope and private commit with the explicit source grammar. Its timeline and log grammar differs from the preview. It accepts neither --limit nor --json. The source also rejects the preview’s commit grammar and has no diff command. The generated Rust API on this site does not describe the preview’s additional storage methods. Start with an empty scratch checkout. Keep the repository database outside it: trial=$(mktemp -d /tmp/gossil-preview.XXXXXX) mkdir -p "$trial/work/app/.agent" "$trial/work/service/.agent" gos vcs init "$trial/history.gossil" gos vcs open --repository "$trial/history.gossil" --checkout source --root "$trial/work" printf 'first plan
' > "$trial/work/app/.agent/plan.md" printf 'first review
' > "$trial/work/service/.agent/review.md" gos vcs add --repository "$trial/history.gossil" --checkout source --path app/.agent/plan.md service/.agent/review.md gos vcs status --repository "$trial/history.gossil" --checkout source --json gos vcs commit --repository "$trial/history.gossil" --checkout source -m "Record agent files" The folders can sit below sibling Git repositories. Gossil tracks the explicitly named paths independently of Git’s index. Here, add chooses paths for tracking; it is not Git-style content staging for each later commit. Edit a tracked file, inspect the change and commit again without re-adding it: printf 'revised plan
' > "$trial/work/app/.agent/plan.md" gos vcs status --repository "$trial/history.gossil" --checkout source --json gos vcs diff --repository "$trial/history.gossil" --checkout source --path app/.agent/plan.md gossil vcs commit --repository "$trial/history.gossil" --checkout source -m "Revise the plan" gos vcs timeline --repository "$trial/history.gossil" --checkout source --limit 10 --json gossil vcs log --repository "$trial/history.gossil" --checkout source --limit 10 --json gos vcs open --repository "$trial/history.gossil" --checkout source A recording commit includes changed tracked paths; these examples do not request a partial commit. log is the alias for timeline. Reopening an existing checkout omits --root; it does not restore or replace working files. No issue, project or author initialization is required for this file workflow. The installed preview passed an isolated smoke test covering the initial empty check-in, two later commits and reopen. This result does not establish release readiness, branching, sync, automatic checkout discovery or full Fossil parity. Issue commands and the server remain unavailable in the preview.

title: Working with repositories
text: In the planned workflow, an agent revises a tracked plan, updates its task and retains a private trace. Review the file diff and task changes together before requesting the integrated operation. The operation checks expected revisions and commits artifacts, derived records, scope, local command history and Gossil checkout heads together. Record-only work creates no file check-in. The shared head selects shared files. An optional private combined head contains those files with the same bytes and attributes, plus selected private files. Each checkout stores its own head pair. Historical review chooses a permitted file head and the exact contributing artifact sets for issues and discussions. Two task-only edits can share one file head, so a check-in hash does not select an issue revision. Complete references also retain required notes, link targets and discussion dependencies. Later arrivals do not rewrite that historical set. Typed issue-to-code links support navigation in both directions across registered Git repositories. They pin commits, blobs and any selected ranges or changes; current filenames and moving branch names cannot supply that guarantee. Required captures preserve permitted target bytes when external code is absent. A descriptor is a structured record naming the versioned target and any selected range. Its transferable encoding remains unfinished; there is no exchange format for applications to implement from this guide yet. Fossil already has immutable ticket history and file check-ins. Gossil’s added contract coordinates exact record boundaries, shared/private file heads and scoped links. Gest contributes the task workflow; one owned transaction strengthens its multi-statement storage helpers. This coordinated operation is planned and is not provided by the current delta diagnostics. The transaction commits changes to the Gossil database. Git commits remain separate source operations, and checkout files are materialized after commit with recovery bookkeeping. A failure then can require checkout recovery while the database history remains committed. Ordinary commands do not automatically combine unrelated file and issue work. See library concepts for the shared model and compare Gossil with Git for the plan/task example and current availability.

title: Working with repositories
section: Separate stored history from the files you edit
text: A repository holds recorded history. A checkout is the folder of files you edit at a selected point in that history. A check-in records a file tree, its parent versions and a comment. A file you edit in the checkout has not become a new check-in until you commit it. Fossil’s concepts guide explains this separation. An artifact is immutable content identified by a hash. A manifest records which file paths and content hashes belong to a check-in. A delta encodes bytes for storage or transfer. It is not itself a user-visible history entry, so the delta tutorial creates no repository history. For Gossil, plan one local repository database with both private and shared material. A team replica receives the shared portion. You do not need a separate personal repository to keep private agent notes. Team replication remains planned.

title: Working with repositories
section: Choose the checkout root and tracked files
text: Choose a root above all the agent files you want in one history. That root may contain several Git repositories. For example, the intended selection could look like this: workspace/ Gossil checkout root AGENTS.md selected by Gossil app/ Git repository src/main.rs selected by Git .agent/plan.md selected by Gossil service/ another Git repository .agent/review.md selected by Gossil The two systems choose files independently. A Git ignore rule for .agent/ does not select those files for Gossil, and Git’s index does not define Gossil’s tracked set. The intended tracking model also permits a Gossil root inside a Git checkout. Choose the root to fit the paths you need. Gossil operations must preserve the nested Git indices, branches and commits. Initialization is intended to select no files automatically. Select files explicitly, then inspect the pending selection before making a check-in. Keep these states distinct: File state Meaning Tracked Selected for version control; edits can enter later check-ins Untracked Present on disk but outside the selected file history Ignored Matches a rule that helps omit unmanaged paths from discovery or recursive addition Missing A tracked path is absent on disk; inspect whether removal was intended An ignore rule is a selection aid, not permission control. Fossil treats explicit paths differently from recursive addition. Recursive addition normally omits dotfiles, while explicitly named ignored files can require confirmation or force. See its add reference. Gossil’s planned default ignore pattern is .git,*/.git,.git/*,*/.git/*. It excludes Git metadata, including .git directories and Git worktree .git files. It must still be possible to see what was selected. The preset does not protect private content by itself.

title: Working with repositories
section: Review a change before recording it
text: The intended daily file workflow follows Fossil: Inspect status to identify edited, added, missing, removed and renamed paths. Read the diff to inspect the actual changes in tracked files. Add new paths, record intentional removals, and record renames. Review status and diff again, then commit one coherent change with a comment. Inspect history to find the resulting check-in and its parent versions. In Fossil, status describes pending changes, while diff compares content. Inspect untracked files separately. A quiet diff of tracked files does not prove that every intended file was added. A commit records the pending changes, unless a file subset was requested. The timeline helps locate earlier work. Removing a path from future versions does not erase its older history. Also distinguish recording a removal or rename from changing the file on disk. Fossil’s remove and move commands have options and settings that control disk effects. Check those effects before using Fossil itself. Gossil will need its own command reference when these operations ship.

title: Working with repositories
text: A branch names a line of check-ins. A fork occurs when work produces competing tips on the same branch. For a plan experiment, a named branch lets you keep the experiment separate while retaining its starting point. See Fossil’s branching guide. Merging combines changes in the checkout. Inspect the result, resolve conflicts and test the affected work before committing the merge. Fossil’s merge reference makes that separate commit step explicit. Downloading another check-in and merging it into your files are different decisions. Gossil’s branches and merge operations remain planned; use your existing Git workflow for source-code work now.

title: Working with repositories
section: Distinguish sharing history from updating a checkout
text: Fossil gives four useful names to repository transfer operations: Operation Purpose in Fossil Clone Create a local repository from an existing one Pull Receive remote history into the local repository Push Send local history to another repository Sync Exchange history in both directions A clone and an open checkout are distinct operations, even where Fossil offers to do both together. A pull receives history. Updating the checkout changes the files you work on. See the clone reference and sharing section. Fossil’s autosync setting can arrange transfers around commands such as commit and update. Know which remote and mode you are using before assuming a local action was shared. Gossil plans to retain replication and autosync workflows, but none of these transfer operations is currently a Gossil command. Gossil adds an explicit private/shared boundary. The planned local write can record a shared issue change and private notes in one database transaction. Either both changes commit or both roll back. Shared history must remain usable without private dependencies. To publish shared material, it is not enough to omit some paths during transfer. The planned synchronization rules define that boundary. Neither an ignore pattern nor Fossil’s private-transfer options establish that Gossil contract.

title: Working with repositories
section: Connect tasks to exact file versions
text: A task describes the work, and a file check-in records selected files. Updating an issue does not have to create a new file check-in. Fossil stores ticket changes as separate artifacts, as its ticket guide explains. Gest is a task and artifact tracker. Gossil adapts this history model to Gest’s tasks, projects and related records. When you record why a change was made, name the exact version. The planned Gossil file reference contains a check-in, relative path and content hash. A Git file reference names its registered repository, full commit, path and blob. A moving branch name alone cannot identify the version an agent read. Uncommitted content needs a captured snapshot if the reference must survive later edits. Exact version references are part of the planned issue and annotation model. A Git object reference also does not guarantee that a recipient has its bytes. The current Gest converters validate decoded records in memory. They cover tasks, projects, authors, artifacts, iterations, tags, notes, relationships, entity tags and iteration tasks. They do not save an issue or create a file reference. Their generated API links give the callable surface. Notebook support remains planned. A notebook is a selected directory and its tracked descendants. It is intended to use selected native file history. SQLAR packages, which are SQLite archives of files, are for interchange rather than a second history system.

title: Working with repositories
text: Before discarding work, inspect the affected paths and keep any unsaved material you still need. Restoring files, backing out a recorded change and undoing a task command have different effects. In Fossil, revert restores files to the checkout baseline or a requested revision. With no file argument it acts on all files. Undo can reverse certain recent working-tree operations, including update, merge and revert. It has one level; commit and checkout clear it. Its dry-run option shows what it would restore. It is not a general backup or an undo for every command. Gossil’s intended undo for Gest command history is separate from undo for operations on checkout files. General recovery commands are not available in the current CLI. For today’s delta diagnostics, preserve the inputs and write to a new output path. Compare the restored bytes before replacing a file.

title: Working with repositories
text: The add and status commands track exact paths and show pending additions or recorded paths with their actual scope. Add stores no file bytes. New paths remain unselected until vcs scope or a library caller makes an explicit scope choice. The private recording API requires immutable private scope for every tracked path. Supply the complete tracked set and the latest checkout view. It rereads all current bytes and executable modes, including changes made since add, and records one complete private snapshot. The shared empty root stays unchanged. An identical tree is a checked no-op, and recording never modifies working files. Use the source walkthrough for explicit scope selection, private commit, edits without re-add and reopen. The separate preview above has a different command contract. Consult development status before assuming that a source feature is installed or released. For a stored history view, library callers can use recorded_timeline. It returns the complete current-first ancestry, including the shared root last. Pending additions and dirty or deleted working files do not alter these records. The source timeline and log commands print those records as compact NDJSON. They require both explicit selectors and a complete matching locator. Their grammar differs from the installed preview above. They accept neither --limit nor --json. These source commands supply no new evidence about the installed preview or its reopen behavior.

title: Working with repositories
section: Glob matching and explicit file tracking
text: The prepared glob module and repository-free test-glob diagnostic inspect pattern lists. They add no wildcard tracking or directory traversal. Continue to pass exact paths to add and scope commands. The focused source checkpoint passed its recorded controls; complete delivery qualification and the installed development preview are separate.

title: Working with repositories
text: Keep Git as the source authority and plan a small explicit selection of agent files for Gossil. Next, try the source private recording walkthrough with disposable files and explicit scopes. For future integrated review, retain the file head and complete issue boundaries together.

title: artifact
text: Parse a cluster, which has no date card, and debit a caller-owned budget. use gossil::artifact::{ ArtifactError, DateProvider, DateProviderError, ParseLimits, parse_artifact_with_usage, }; struct NoDates; impl DateProvider for NoDates { async fn julianday(&self, _: Option ) -> Result , DateProviderError> { Ok(None) } } let mut input = b"M aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa\n".to_vec(); let checksum = gossil::artifact_checksum::md5(&input); input.extend_from_slice(b"Z "); for byte in checksum { input.extend_from_slice(format!("{byte:02x}").as_bytes()); } input.push(b'\n'); let mut remaining = ParseLimits { input_bytes: 4096, cards: 100, owned_bytes: 8192, entries: 100, }; let (_, usage) = parse_artifact_with_usage(&input, remaining, &NoDates).await?; assert_eq!(usage.input_bytes, input.len()); assert_eq!(usage.cards, 2); assert_eq!(usage.entries, 1); remaining.input_bytes -= usage.input_bytes; remaining.cards -= usage.cards; remaining.owned_bytes -= usage.owned_bytes; remaining.entries -= usage.entries; assert_eq!(remaining.cards, 98); The successful charges fit the supplied limits, so these subtractions cannot underflow. On an error, stop and discard the enclosing operation state.
